speakeroldname: Mr. R. W. MAYHEW (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Just before the house adjourned at eleven o'clock last evening the minister was asked a number of questions by hon. members on the other side of the house and on this side in connection with rentals generally and particularly about the hardships created for returned soldiers because they were not able to get into their houses. I should like to make a brief statement in that connection.
Rent control is one of the most important controls that we have had, because that one item probably affects the cost of living more

than any other single consideration. But it is also one of the most difficult controls to manage, for the reason that there is no general pattern that one can follow. You have to take into consideration the type of house, the character of the people involved, both landlord and tenant, and the city. There is really no definite way in which we can regulate it so as to suit everyone. Therefore there have been and there always will be hardship cases, or cases that must be dealt with outside the regulations.
At first we set up in each district a magistrate with one or two other commissioners to help to regulate rents and to afford a place where the landlord or the tenant might appeal for justice. That was not a perfect plan, but it worked, and it did help to smooth out the regulations considerably. More recently, just last fall, a different type of organization was established, one which I believe did more good than many people give credit for. I refer to the commissioners, of whom a number were set up all over Canada, and they were to deal with the hardship cases only.
You must adopt, not a legal but rather a humane approach to the settlement of differences between landlord and tenant. I found in my own home town when I returned, a number of cases in which landlord and tenant were ready to fight, but after going into the homes and talking things over with them I was successful in a number of cases in getting the differences settled.
The government last fall set up just such a commission. They set up rent-control men and gave them a chance to go and see both landlord and tenant, as well as the type of place in which people were living, and in that way these men knew better how to handle the situation.
Someone said last night that it was not very successful. I assure you that it has not been one hundred per cent successful, but if it cured twenty or twenty-five per cent of the cases, it was in my opinion a success, and it did relieve at least twenty-five per cent of those who made appeal. Their cases have been settled to the satisfaction of both landlord and tenant.
As regards returned soldiers or any others who bought houses and were not able to get into them, such persons invariably bought with the knowledge that the regulation existed before they entered into the deal, and consequently there is little we can do about it. I have spoken to many of them and they argued in this way: Well, probably the rent control was on, but they thought that they could reason with the tenant and so get into their own homes. They were willing to take

Transitional Measures Act
a chance, and they had this at stake as well, that they were buying the house before the high bulge came in prices, so that they could get the house at a little lower price than if they would have waited for a year or so. That was their reasoning.
There are many returned soldiers who have not been able to get into their own homes and no one regrets that fact more than the members of this house, but there does not seem to be anything that we can do about it.
Last night a number of individual cases were presented to the committee. As part of my duty as parliamentary assistant to the minister I have been listening to these special cases day after day. Hardly a day passes that I have not three or four to deal with, and I should be only too happy if any hon. member would bring such cases to my attention so that we may see what we can do by referring the matter to the rent control people to see if we can get the commission to smooth out the trouble as far as possible.
It is necessary to keep on the control for a time at least, and it is also necessary, for us to do everything we can to alleviate conditions where hardship cases exist.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Last night I asked a question about the relief being given to returned soldiers. We have heard the parliamentary assistant's explanation, but it does not go far enough. It is not sufficient to say that the returned soldier bought his place knowing that he might not be able to get into it. The fact is that the fellow was overseas and he came back to Canada expecting that at least he would get a place to live in, and he must do something to help himself. If he cannot rent a place he must buy one. I do not think it is a sufficient answer to say that because he bought the place knowing that he could not move into it immediately he is not entitled to relief.
I believe that deep down, every one of us, without allowing politics to play any part at all in the matter, is of the view that the returned man is entitled to relief now. It is quite some time since the end of the war. Why should not the government fix a deadline at December 31, 1947, or some date prior to that, at any rate some deadline, so that if the returned man had already bought the house and was owner of it at that date he should have relief?
As the parliamentary assistant says, many of them are not able to get into their own houses. If the department knows what the problem is, and there cannot possibly be more than two or three thousand of these cases throughout the country, it is not a sufficient 5849-144i
answer to say that we cannot do anything about it. I feel that we should have some assurance from the minister now-we shall be satisfied with an assurance from him, because we know that if the minister gives us an assurance he will deal with the matter-that some steps will be taken to widen the act on behalf of returned men so that some amendment will go forward to the commissioners which will give them an opportunity to deal with the situation on the basis of equity for the returned men.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Notwithstanding anything contained in any other order of the board, the landlord of any housing accommodation owned by him prior to January 1, 1947, may make an application to a commissioner for an order permitting the landlord to recover possession in accordance with the law of the province in which such accommodation is situated. I am informed that 8,400 applications have been made under this order, and of that number 2,411 have been granted.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Of the number who got relief, 2,411 of the 8,400 applications, how many are from New Brunswick and how many from the county of Restigouche? As far as I know there have been a dozen or so applications in my county and no landlord has had any relief.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is the same in Toronto..

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is the same all over-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Last night I referred to this question of hardship. The first client for whom I appeared was a tenant, a man with a grown-up family who had been occupying the house for years. The landlord happened to be a veteran who had a wife and' family, and he was living in a little shack, twelve by twelve or something like that, which had no foundation, running water or toilet. If that is not a case of hardship, I do not know what is. It is about the most extreme case of hard>-ship that could be brought to the attention of the commissioner. But when we came before the commissioner, although he was a tenant- he remarked during the hearing that he was a tenant and a tenant man-I think he was fair just the same. But when he looked at the other side of the picture and a certain paragraph in that order in council was pointed out, it was found that the landlord, in order to succeed, must practically get a place for the tenant. He must establish that there will be no hardship on the tenant, or practically none. I see some of the officials here making signs indicating the negative, but that is the interpretation the commissioner placed1 on it, and it appeared to be borne out by the text
Transitional Measures Act

of the order in council. The result was that in my community hardly any landlord received any relief.
In the little villages and hamlets I do not believe there is any necessity for continuing this rental regulation with regard to housing accommodation. It is different in the towns. In the smaller places-and I could cite instances of what has happened-in most cases that have been brought to my attention this regulation serves as a protection to an unreasonable tenant. I know of cases in which houses have been purchased by bona fide landlords with a view to occupation. A middle-aged woman bought a house a couple of years ago with a view to occupying it herself, with her crippled husband. She wrote to me about it nearly a year ago. I told her she had better see a lawyer, and she did1. The lawyer advised her to make application to evict the tenant because he was obnoxious. As a matter of fact the tenant had bumped into the corner of the house with his car and had caused damage of a dollar or so. This lawyer advised her that she would have a good case, and they went to court. Before they went to court they called in another lawyer.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The legal firm will soon have the house.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The result of it was that 'her case was dismissed, and properly so. It *cost her plenty of money. Incidentally this *woman had earned the money by cooking in lumber camps. When this recent regulation was passed she obtained an application form from some justice of the peace, sent it in and a day was set for the hearing. In the meantime she came to me again and asked me to represent her at the hearing, which I agreed to do. I told her to come at two o'clock, and the lady was late. Her watch had stopped. She reached my office about two minutes late. We ran to the place of hearing, which was across the street, and we found that the commissioner had closed the court. The tenant was there with his solicitor at two o'clock, and the case was dismissed.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: He is a bachelor, I guess.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Well, the poor lady burst into tears. The commissioner would not open the court.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Don't make us cry here.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
You don't need to if you don't feel like it, although it is a sad case. On various occasions before, I had been successful in obtaining possession under the section with regard to subdivision. This house

happened to be a good-sized one; and the owner had contemplated using one flat herself and allowing her son to use the other. So I said, "Perhaps this is the shortest cut.. We might make application for subdivision." In the past I had been successful. When we had an office in Moncton the gentleman in charge there was sympathetic and granted applications almost as a matter of course when there was sufficient floor space to warrant it. Well, it took quite a while, but eventually two gentlemen came from Saint John and I gave them all the information I had on it. It was necessaiy for them to go and see the place, which is out in the country. They did so, and they wrote back to me saying that they did not think this woman had the means to make the alterations. She could not put toilets in both places because there is no water system in that little country place; consequently her application would be dismissed. That is the situation. Incidentally, one of those gentlemen told me that they had had rather more stringent instructions as to this matter of subdivision. There had been abuses in the past.
That is not the first time these officers who act in a judicial capacity have told us frankly that they have had instructions. A county court, judge in my riding, who is fair in every respect, on some occasions humbly expressed the view, "Well, I should like to grant your application but I have received a report from the Saint John office that the government wants this and that, and I do not feel justified in granting it". The objection I am taking is to interference on the part of someone advising these men who sit in a judicial capacity as to what they should or should not do.
As I stated before, I feel that in my community this new order in council has not served any great purpose. Why should it be that a person who bought a house in good faith over a year ago, for personal occupation, cannot get possession? Why can he not get possession as he could before July 25, 1945? The fact that he cannot does not provide more living accommodation for the people as a whole. He wants his house, but if he gets it he will vacate some other place. I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce when the matter came up last year referred to extreme cases in which a move like this would put a family out, or perhaps two families. But there are few such cases in the smaller communities. As I said before, I agree that the rental control should be continued for large cities and towns; and there are some people in my own home town who have expressed in no uncertain terms their appreciation of what has been done in this matter. But I say again that in little country

Transitional Measures Act
places this regulation serves only to protect unreasonable tenants. I pointed out one case, and I could point out many others where I feel that the rental regulation has worked injustice on certain classes of people. I hope something will be done in the near future to remedy the situation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said he wanted to know how many cases there were in New Brunswick. Under this order about which I just spoke, 143 applications were made and 35 have been granted. The hon. member said that rent control should be off in the small places. Our experience is that there is just as great a shortage of houses in the small cities and towns as there is in the large ones. We know there is hardship, but we have to look at the over-all picture. I can assure the committee that our control officers are daily searching to find some way of relieving cases where there is hardship.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have not said anything about this control business; but I can tell you this, that controls will never get houses built. I live in a city where the city owns the street railway system, and I doubt very much if any other agency since 1921 has done as much for housing as has the city of Toronto, and particularly with its street car and bus services extending to the outlying districts of the city, urban, suburban and rural.
Following the last war the cheap light and power and transportation development in Toronto led to the building of houses. It is intended by this measure to extend these controls to sixty days after parliament is called, or to the end of March, 1949. That is a political procedure, to tide the government over the next election, no doubt.
I have seen these controls in operation in our city, and I can tell the committee they will not function, so far as the building of houses is concerned. Today those materials which are available are being used for the building of banks, skyscrapers, theatres, and other non-essential buildings. And let me say that the rent courts are the biggest farce I have ever seen. I have had some contact with some of them, and I can tell the committee that when some tenants get into a house they sublet rooms and tear the place to pieces and do three or four times more, damage than they pay the owner in rents. Then some of these tenants are profiteering by charging 810, $12 or $14 a week for rooms. The landlord gets a little or nothing out of it. I was head of a city at one time, and I believe I know as much about housing as do a great many others in the committee.
I did not mean to reflect on the hon. member for Parkdale; he is a valuable member, and knows well the conditions in his constituency. He knows, too, how these rent controls have affected all sections of the city of Toronto.
Will this system of controls build houses? I say it will not build a single house. The assessment rolls of Toronto show that before the war more than sixty-six per cent of the people there owned their own homes. Many of those houses had been purchased at high interest rates. Some of the purchasers were soldiers who went to the war, and when they came back they found they could not get into (heir own houses; they were occupied by tenants who were profiteering at the expense of the soldiers. These were soldiers who gave up their jobs and who went to fight tho battles of those who stayed at home. I can assure the committee that if this control system now to be extended for a year would bring about the building of more houses it would be an entirely different matter.
Mind you, I sympathize with the government, with a problem like this on its hands; but I called attention to that problem away back last spring. There was a conference held at Geneva in 1947, beginning on February 7, but we did not hear one word about this austerity program until November 17. If the government would give some encouragement to small builders with materials and labour who would build houses, and if it would give some encouragement or some incentive to commercial landlords who would build commercial buildings or stores and small apartments in the commercial districts, it would be doing something worth while. But nothing of that kind has been done.
Coming down to November 17, we find the government realizing that winter was coming on. When I saw that the government had done nothing between February 7 and November 17, and when I realized that winter was coming on, I asked the government as early as last June about this housing problem. I knew what was going to happen. We were going to be back just where we were after the last war-only this time it would be more serious. The lack of housing today is three times greater than it was at that time.
What did the government do ? It announced a new Geneva policy on November 17, and all that kind of thing. It hamstrung small and large business. Will houses be built under this program? I say they will not.
We hear a good deal about the rent courts, and we have seen what they have done right here in Ottawa. Only a short time ago we read about a family who were arraigned in court because they had1 not looked after their chil-
Transitional Measures Act

dren. How could anyone look after children in the circumstances under which some people re housed? I am not here to justify the actions of those people, but I can say that there are hundreds of people like them in every city of Canada. People are living in hovels and in shacks of all kinds. And these conditions exist while we sit here in the House of Commons even near this district.
This is one of the greatest problems we will ever face in our lives. How can the people stand it. I do not place the blame on any particular government, but it must be realized1 that the housing situation in this country is deplorable. The birds of the air have somewhere to go, but the poor people can go nowhere. They have no houses-nothing. Public health is at stake.
I am not here to criticize any government -far from it, because this housing situation has existed for a long time. But I will say that the rent courts which have been established are the biggest farce I ever saw in my life. I have had something to do with them, and I have seen some of them in operation. There is no justice in some of them. The sooner we stop calling in county court judges for this kind of work, the better. I am opposed to the policy of using the members of the judiciary for whom I have the greatest respect, and who command the respect of every citizen, for this rent court work. This rental situation is apt to hold them up to contempt and ridicule.
Rentals administrators and county judges are brought here to Ottawa from other places. What are they doing? Do hon. members think they are doing a good job? I fail to see it. Many cases have been heard before them, but I can tell the committee this, that in the experience I have had with this matter I have seen profiteering by tenants, and the landlord lias had no chance at all. He is the forgotten man, and in that respect is in the same position as the returned soldier. I know some of those tenants are operating in violation of civic building by-laws. They proceed to build as in industry, and even in the residential district some of them carry on factory operations.
Is it any wonder no one wants to put money into housing? Is it any wonder so many mortgages are being foreclosed, with real estate in a condition of that kind? ITe cannot expect people or corporations to put money into building small houses, or to relieve the housing situation, both urban and suburban. We cannot expect them to enter into building in a commercial way and build small houses so as to aid new housing and stop profiteering.

I have never seen the like of it. And when we visit some of these places wre see soldiers who suffered in the war living in badly ventilated- apartments, small rooms or shacks, some of which are fire traps.
We will never have building unless we eliminate some of the housing controls. If the steel and1 lumber and concrete and other building materials which have been used in the building of banks, theatres, warehouses and all that kind1 of thing, had been used for housing purposes, we would have got somewhere.
This is a serious state of affairs, even right here in the city of Ottawa. Some members of parliament are familiar with the situation, one that is common to almost every city of Canada. The government's policy should have been announced last spring. Mr. Truman, across the line, announced that they were going away from controls, but he started it again in September. However, we made no announcement until November 17. This decontrol business was mixed up with Geneva agreements and Hyde Park and other things like that. I can tell you this, that I do not know anyone who wants to go into the building of houses at the present time.
On the island of Montreal proceedings were taken under the Railways Act to relieve the housing situation. A suburban service was inaugurated thirty years ago, and we can see what it has done for Montreal, both in winter and in summer. In Toronto we have not had the same opportunity, although we are entitled to it. I say we should have a steam suburban service which would permit commutation tickets from Toronto to Oakville and Brampton and other outlying points. I know the hon. member for Peel will agree with that. The housing situation was relieved by the action of the T.T.C. in serving the suburbs. Housing with civic services is largely a civic problem. The railw-ay commission was required' by law to investigate these matters of a suburban service without any application being made. If we had1 more help from the railway commission and better service was provided the housing situation would be remedied in York, Peel and Ontario counties as it was remedied after the last war.
I do not want to criticize the government all the time because I know the difficulty the war and reconversion caused in getting materials and labour and all that kind of thing, but the time has come when there should be some revision of these rental boards. Thejr are very largely a farce and as far as I can see there is very little justice. To bring

Transitional Measures Act
the judiciary into this situation is a retrograde step from the point of view of law and order.
What are we going to do about it? Spring is coming on and something will have to be done. The government wants to turn housing back to the provinces and the municipalities. The first duty of the federal government is to look after the health, wealth, prosperity and happiness of its citizens. Housing should be a federal problem, not a municipal or provincial problem. That is how it is handled in Britain and in the United States where money is advanced to the states and municipalities.
I think it is a large order to extend this to March 31, 1949, or sixty days after the house meets. I fail to see how it is going to help the housing situation. The government of the day should provide assistance to municipalities during the next six months in order to tide things over the following winter. I saw the situation from February 7 until November 17 when nothing was done. Last June I saw this hard winter coming and I suggested that some assistance should be given for milk, bread and coal. That would have been a good thing because we did not know they were going to make a leap in the dark like they did on November 17.
I doubt whether we can do much by legislation. Certainly the government's suggestion to extend these controls to March 31, 1949, is not going to function very well. It is going to lead to more confusion, and lack of building and of private building. Builders will not want to build this spring and it will do considerable harm and prevent the building of small houses by small builders for next winter.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is one of those questions about which much can be said by both sides. It is unfortunate indeed that the interests of the landlord and tenant are diametrically opposed. If the government will not do what we propose, that is, provide more low rental housing units as quickly as possible, then I suppose they can only do the best they can for the greater number of people. I imagine that in this particular instance the greater number of people are the tenants. While my hon. friends to my right have said a great deal about veterans who are landlords, we might point out that a great many tenants are also veterans.
It is a coincidence that just before I came into the chamber I picked up a letter from a veteran, and as some hon. members have been putting personal matters on the record perhaps I might put this one on. This veteran is the owner of a modern house in a
good residential district. He purchased the house with the aid of his war service gratuities and re-establishment grant. Under the present legislation he cannot occupy the premises and is forced to live in a house which is far from modern.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: When did he purchase it?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: He does not say, and I am afraid that that is the difficulty so far as the regulations are concerned. As I have indicated he lives in a house which is far from modern and which is located seven blocks from a street car, and then he must take a fifteen minute walk to his work. This man had four years service in the second world war. In the letter he gives some personal details which I can leave out, but he underlines this question at the end of this letter: What is being done to remedy this situation? I presume I can write back to him and quote the words of the parliamentaiy assistant and say, "Nothing."

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to give support to the principles put forward: by the hon. member for Broadview when he called the government's attention to the situation which exists in the larger cities of Canada. The housing situation is crucial; it is Canada's No.2 problem. In my opinion it comes closely behind communism; in fact it is creating communism. Dissatisfaction and discontent are being created because of the housing regulations and restrictions and the lack of accommodation.
There is a great principle at stake which I know the Minister of Justice will recognize. The federal government have taken the responsibility of putting on these, controls. Any person who has knowledge of the situation agrees that they have resulted in a restriction of housing and a restriction of building, especially for rent. The government have imposed these controls and it is their policy. They have refused to acknowledge the free enterprise system in so far as housing is concerned, and therefore there is only one other course of action they can take and that is to enter into the housing field themselves.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I know the hon. gentleman would like to be right. He says that these regulations have affected the building of houses, but I would tell him that no house built since January 1947 is under control in any way, shape or form, either as to the amount of rent paid or the tenancy.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am glad to have the parliamentary assistant correct me, but the fact remains that there is a great deal of uncertainty in the housing field. The number oi houses built since January 1, 1947, is not very
Transitional Measures Act

large and I would imagine that ninety-eight per cent of the houses in Canada are still under control to some extent.
I was developing the argument that if the government insists upon the continued control of housing and rentals there is only one course open to them if this problem is to be solved. They must either build houses or subsidize those wrho can build them, namely, the provinces and the municipalities. I repeat that if the government intend to continue housing controls they must subsidize the provinces and the municipalities in their housing program. Their policies have already driven the two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec into the housing field, the two provinces which have been denied, through the government's mistaken policies, the grants in aid which are paid to the other seven provinces. The two central and most populous provinces have been driven into the housing field by the policies of this government, and I say that this government should today start to return to Ontario and Quebec the moneys collected in lieu of grants, so that they can be distributed by the governments of these two provinces through the municipalities, chiefly Montreal, Quebec, Toronto, Hamilton, London, Windsor and Ottawa-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And Kingston.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And Kingston, to be allocated to a municipal housing program. If the government are going to collect these moneys which are due to the provinces they should return them forthwith to those provinces which have been driven into the housing field.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Who would have the corporation tax in those provinces under my hon. friend's plan?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The federal government is now collecting a portion of the tax in the event of those two provinces signing an agreement with the dominion, and it is withholding that amount until then. That is one of the reasons for the government's surplus. Isn't there some $180,000,000 involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend surely realizes that under the present plan the corporation tax collected on corporations in provinces other than the two central provinces is 35 per cent, while it is only 30 per cent in the two central provinces.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What would five per cent of the corporation tax amount to in Ontario and Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I could get it. It would be very great.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It would not be equal to the amount which would be payable to those provinces under a signed agreement with the federal government, would it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I doubt whether it would be quite as much as that, but it might be more.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I gravely doubt it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is up to them.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, no; it is up to the federal government to give the provinces taxation rights in certain fields. However, I shall not get into an argument with the minister over that at the moment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what we are considering now is P.C. 9029, wartime leasehold regulations as amended. There will be ample opportunity under the Department of Reconstruction and Supply to discuss on three or four items the question of housing when the minister will be here to answer, and I suggest that we should defer this discussion until then. We would like to see all the lumber go into the building of houses. It would relieve the situation. I can only assure my hon. friend that rent control will be prosecuted with the utmost intensity and justice and sympathy in order to be fair to everybody. I cannot promise more than that and I do not think you can get more out of it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The point raised by the parliamentary assistant is in order. The committee should deal specifically with the wartime leasehold regulations.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was endeavouring to develop the point, Mr. Chairman, that these restrictions are aggravating the housing shortage and will continue to do so. I fully acknowledge the difficulty in which the federal government is placed today and the difficulties of both landlords and tenants. Coming from an urban constituency where the problem is very acute, I am perfectly aware of the difficulties, which work hardships on both sides. I am not arguing for just one side, but I am saying that it is the continuation of controls that makes necessary a housing policy sponsored and financed by the federal government. The parliamentary assistant has mentioned the minister of reconstruction. I was just coming to him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Wait until he comes in.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The situation is acute. But I see you are about to rise, Mr. Chairman, and so I will withhold what I had to say on that. I have advocated as strongly as I can that those hundreds of millions of dollars should

Transitional Measures Act
now be placed in the hands of the governments of Ontario and Quebec to assist in the housing programs into which they have been forced by the continuation of these controls.
I will close by venturing to suggest that even those in the position of tenants today who are enjoying the protection of rent control will be the first to insist on a clear title and absolute freedom when they come to purchase property of their own because they are keenly aware of the situation in which their landlords are placed today. There is nothing to be gained politically by arguing this question, because there are people on both sides to be offended no matter which side you take, but I say it is the greatest problem in Canada today and this government should bend very effort to its solution.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: A short time ago the parliamentary assistant read from an amending order, I take it, of last year. Would he give us the number and date of that order and tell us whether its provisions were not predicated upon the factor of hardship?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The order number is 753, and it was predicated on the basis of hardship.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not want to be misled. I do not suggest that the parliamentary assistant is endeavouring to mislead the committee but we have not had an answer yet as to whether the minister is willing to consider extending this amending order to make some provision for the veteran on the basis of hardship. I refer to the veteran who has bought and paid for his house before December 31, 1947, and whose hardship consists of not being able to maintain himself and of not being able to hold the house if he cannot get into it himself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If the veteran owned the house before he enlisted he can get possession *without difficulty.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is not the point.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The other relief is the one I have just read. A further one is that if it is a new house built since January, 1947, he can get into it. If he cannot comply with any of those conditions he is rated as an ordinary citizen. I wish we could do something more about it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not want to labour this. The fact of the matter is that the parliamentary assistant says nothing can be done. I think something can be done if the minister is prepared to give some assurance that it will be looked into with the purpose of trying to find hardship that will work out in favour of
the veteran who cannot afford not to be in control of his own house. The order is acting against the interests of the men who are not able to help themselves.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I can assure the hon. gentleman that if he can offer us a solution to the problem we shall be very happy to consider it; but at the present time there are more returned soldiers than landlords, and often returned soldiers are competing against each other to get into the house. It is a most difficult proposition. I assure the hon. member it is being dealt with as sympathetically and as intensely as we can possibly do. Let anyone give us a solution to the problem and we shall be glad to entertain it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I suggest to the minister that he give serious consideration to the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska and by the other hon. members who have protested against this regulation which provides that a man who buys a house for the purpose of getting into it is refused permission to occupy it.
The parliamentary assistant to the minister has said that he can do very little about the matter. He does not say that nothing can be done about it. If I recall aright, the wording of the resolution says that if a person who buys a house under these circumstances wants to get into it, he has to show that he has greater need for that house than the occupant. The onus is on him to show that he has a greater need for it than the occupant. What I fail to understand is this. Why should a man who has bought a house for the purpose of occupying it be obliged to show that he has a greater need for it than the person who is occupying it? Surely it should be sufficient for him to show that as he owns the house he has a need as great as the person who occupies it. If you are bound to continue these regulations, then they might well be modified to the extent I have suggested; the man who owns a house should be allowed to have possession of it if he can show he has as great a need as the person who is in possession. Perhaps some hardship would be created, but I do not think the cost of living would be raised if you did away with this regulation altogether.
The committee was informed this afternoon that there had been only some 8,000 applications all over Canada. These applications must represent most of the people who have suffered from this regulation. In New Brunswick there have been only 143 applications. If all these applications were granted I do not believe the cost of living would be raised to
2264
Transitional Measures Act

any extent; and I think justice would be done and the principles of law and of free enterprise as we understand them would be lived up to if you would let a man occupy a house when he has bought it and wants to move into it with his family.
I have received quite a number of letters. I hold in my hand a letter which was written me in January. It is from a woman who is badly in need of getting into her house with her family. She says:
My husband is a veteran with six years' service, four years overseas. When he came home he bought a house, putting every cent he had into it. Now we hear that the controls may be kept on another year.
We are nearly crazy living in a small four-roomed apartment with three children, who are really suffering because of the way we are living. They can't play, and every time they come in or out the landlord or other tenants scold them. We have to pay $45 per month, and you can imagine what that does to my husband's salary.
He has a small salary. I continue with the letter:
The rents are very low in the house we bought, hardly more than enough to cover expenses. One of our tenants has told us that they have a home (outside the city) but while they can have a large six-room flat -with garage and large yard for $15 per month . . .
While the veteran who owns the house with a small salary, a wife and three children is obliged to pay $45 because he cannot get into his own house. Conditions of that kind are not fair or right and should not be permitted for one minute.
I have received quite a number of complaints also from persons who own houses and rent them. Their complaint is that they are not getting a fair return on the money they have invested. They say they are not getting enough of a return to make necessary improvements to their houses. The regulation should be such as to enable a person to get sufficient from his investment to meet the cost of repairs, taxes, heating and so on, and give him a fair return on his investment.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Following the point
raised by the hon. member for St. John-Albert may I say I now have the text of this order, and my submission is that the relief granted by it is much more insignificant than was indicated by the hon. member. Not only must the landlord show hardship, but at the hearing, according to subsection 6, the commissioner may require such further information- and I skip some parts that are immaterial and go down to (b) which asks for the circumstances of the tenant and the nature of the real hardship which would be suffered

by the tenant and his family if the occupation was allowed1. Whenever any application of this nature is made the tenant who refuses to go out will come into court or come before the commissioner and put up a hard luck story. Naturally he will say that he has hunted around the town and the community for the last two or three months and has not been able to find a suitable place. He will say that he has a large family. That constitutes hardship, and it must be taken into consideration by the commissioner. I have a case in mind. A veteran wanted to get into his house. He had two children. The other fellow had six grown-up children. The commissioner said, "You are asking me to put them out. He has six of a family; you have two. What is the advantage of putting out six to give room to two?" When I went into court I thought I had a good' case. I heard the interpretation placed on the regulation by a man who was not a legal man, but I thought he interpreted the regulation properly. The landlord must do more than show that he is in hard circumstances. When he goes into court he has a roof over his head1, and he wants to throw another person out. Naturally the answer of the court or the judge is this: "You have a place now; you are fairly comfortable. You are asking me to throw this other person out." The other person says that this constitutes hardship, and it is hard enough, it is true-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You should have read the regulations first.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I say the regulation is practically worthless. I have run across the occasion where the tenant has said, "If you let me stay in until the first of May I will get out". On such occasions the commissioner has mad'e an order, but in most cases where orders have been made it is done by consent such as I have indicated. The tenant has practically agreed to get out at a future date. If the tenant says, "I cannot find a place, I have no place to go", I do not see any justification under the regulation for the commissioner to evict.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
May I answer the hon. member for St. John-Albert? In the first case, where a man might go and buy a house and get possession of it, you would be letting someone in and turning out a returned soldier. That is probably what would happen in your first case. In your second case, where a man says he is not getting what is fair and reasonable for his house, he can appeal to the board for an adjustment, and a good many thousands of cases have been adjusted.

Transitional Measures Act

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It seems to me that the only solution of the rental problem is more houses. There is no other answer to it. I know that the present minister and his assistant are not responsible for building houses, but they are asking parliament to extend their powers of controls over rentals. Can the minister give us some idea as to how long these controls are to continue?
I am not rising to make criticism one way or another. I have no criticisms to make. I do not see what can be done except what is being done. The situation exists as it is, and the government is trying to handle it the best way it can.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: A pretty poor best.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That may be subject to criticism too. I have letters from tenants making complaints; I have about an equal number from landlords making complaints, and it is difficult to satisfy both. I do not think the case which the hon. member for St. John-Albert brought to the attention of the minister was the strongest he might have made. There are many cases much worse than that. Here is a man with two children and four rooms to live in. I am not taking the side of the tenant, and perhaps he is a pretty fortunate man. I am surprised in one way, and I know it is because of the lack of building materials, that so many four-room homes have been built throughout the country. I believe that if the time ever comes when there is no shortage of housing you will be able to buy four-room houses for a song. That, however, is another matter, and I know I am not entirely within the rules in bringing it up.
Can the minister tell us how many building permits were issued in 1947 as compared with 1946 and 1945? You may think, Mr. Chairman, that is not in order, but that is the only way I can see whereby we can discover what the situation is and when perhaps there will be some relief in the way of lifting of controls. How long will it last? We are asked to grant continued power of control. People do not know whether the controls are to come off or whether they will be left on this year and another year as well. We should have some answer to that question. Is it expected that they will last for another year or another five or ten years? If building has dropped off, then there is some reason for it, and the government is not going to the root of the problem unless it discovers that reason, because the only solution of the problem is more houses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Two questions have been asked. One is, how many permits were issued in 1945, 1916 and 1917? That question should 5849-145J
be directed to the Minister of Reconstruction and) Supply who will be coming on, I hope, in a few minutes and will be able to give that information. As far as the length of time is concerned, we are asking for the extension of these controls to the end of the fiscal year, that is the end of March, 1949. Whether they are extended beyond that will depend on the will of the house.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
This discussion we have had in the last few hours is like the discussion we had a year ago in this house, and apparently no progress has been made. A year ago we discussed1 the problem of the veteran owner who could not get into his house because of rental restrictions, and the ministers at that time expressed great sympathy for the veteran. I remember the Minister of Finance saying that it was a very constructive discussion, and I should think many members of the house thought that something might be done about the matter in the intervening time. But apparently nothing has been done at all, and the reasons given by the parliamentary assistant today are precisely the reasons given a year ago.
The unfortunate fact is that we have here a real hardship on these veterans and it is the responsibility of the government. I do not think it is at all satisfactory that a whole year should have passed and that we should be given the same answers now as those we got a year ago.
The hon. member who has just spoken has mentioned one way of relieving the situation, which is to get more houses, and that is the responsibility of the government. As I understand, they have not succeeded in the past year in increasing the number of rental houses which will be available. It has not increased substantially, and I find at page 2234 of Hansard of April 21 of last year that the minister suggested that the only way out was to increase the number of units available.
Last year the hon. member for Eglinton offered to the government another way in which the number of housing units available might be materially increased. He gave it as his opinion, which is a valuable one, since he knows a great deal about housing, that by this means you would bring into the market a considerable amount of rental housing. His suggestion was to amend the regulations with respect to eviction from shared accommodation so as to enable a large number of people in Canada who have accommodation now too large for them to take in tenants, with the assurance that they will be able to evict those tenants if they prove to be unsatisfactory.
Transitional Measures Act

According to the present regulation they cannot be evicted except on six months' notice, and1 it was suggested that if that period were reduced to one month it would open up a great field of available living accommodation which heretofore has not been tapped. The hon. member for Eglinton moved that as an amendment, but the government refused to accept it just as they refused to accept his amendment last year with respect to the veteran home owner.
If we are to go on from year to year without any progress in this matter, surely that second suggestion of the hon. member for Eglinton should be, I was going to say accepted by the government, but certainly gone into very carefully indeed-. Perhaps it has been gone into. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant can give us a statement as to why the suggestion has not been taken into consideration and that field opened up so as to relieve the housing shortage.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver-]! urrard says that nothing has been done to relieve the situation. I would point out to the committee that last year 78,000 houses were built in Canada. Before the war our normal capacity was in the neighborhood of 32,000. I happen to know that, because I had something to do with the building trades. Our capacity was around about 32,000 houses before the war, but last year we built 78,000 in Canada.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How many couples were married? [DOT]

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: One hundred thousand.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In October last, in the hon. member's own city of Vancouver, there were 5,500 wartime houses under construction. I think that since that date a further 1,500 have been added to that to have them ready to relieve those housed in the old Vancouver hotel. When Canadians have stepped up their production of housing by nearly three times, I think there must be something or somebody behind that accomplishment, directing it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The parliamentary assistant has not yet answered my question. I heard the hon. member for Regina City call out, asking what the net family formations were in that same year. It is my understanding that, on the whole, we are losing ground in providing accommodation for Canadian families. How many of the 78,000 houses, to which the parliamentary assistant referred, were rental houses? I remember distinctly that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply in the .housing debate last year said that his chief
JMr. Merritt.]
worry in connection with housing was that rental units were not being provided. A large number of these 78,000 houses are of no use to people who can only afford to rent. I should like to hear the parliamentary assistant tell the committee what consideration has been given to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Eglinton last year which was to the effect that if you reduce the period of notice which must be given in the case of shared accommodation, you will open up in the cities of Canada a large field of accommodation which has not been tapped' so far. What is the answer to that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Thirty-seven per cent of the urban population live in shared accommodation; and unless they are obnoxious, they require the six months' notice. But if they are obnoxious they can be evicted on much shorter notice. They can be evicted under the regulations of the provincial government which provide for short notice and on the grounds of incompatibility.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Of course that is not an answer to my question. My question is this; what investigation has been made, following the suggestion moved as an amendment by the hon. member for Eglinton last year, to ascertain how much new housing accommodation would be made available by a reduction in the period of eviction from six months to one month.
Mr. 'ILSLEY: I was in the discussion last year, Mr. Chairman, and I remember the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton. While I have not been engaged in this department since that time, and am not at the present time, I understand that consideration has been given to that suggestion. The suggestion is based upon a theory that you would gain more accommodation than you would lose if you allowed the owner of the house to turn those tenants out on short notice. That is merely a theory, and it is a theory with which those who have studied the matter do not agree. It is not susceptible of proof. On the contrary it is believed that, with the national income what it is, for ten rooms that you would gain by the application of that theory you would lose 100, because the landlords would turn the tenants out and would not let anyone else in; and the fact that they could turn people out suddenly would not cause them to let others in.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That was not the suggestion made by the hon. member for Eglinton. I have it here and it may be found at page 2250 of Hansard of 1947. I will not read it

Transitional Measures Act
all. It referred to this question of freeing shared accommodation from eviction control, and the last few words of the amendment are as follows:
. . . where the tenancy thereof is created after the date of coming into force of this act.
So it will be seen that his suggestion would not have freed any present accommodation from the present six months' notice legislation and would not have lost any you now have. His suggestion would have applied only to new shared accommodation being made available because of this suggestion, just in the same way as you have released from control houses coming into occupation after January 1, 1947.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The administrative difficulty there is this. Suppose there are five tenants in one house, and one room becomes vacant. Then the tenant who goes into that room can be turned out without notice or with very short notice, while the other tenants in the other four rooms are entitled to their six months' notice. The discrimination that arises there between tenants is regarded as most undesirable.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I must say that explanation does not satisfy me; because if you apply your new order only to new accommodation and not to old accommodation becoming free, only to a completely new building where you never had shared accommodation before, you would never get the difficulty which the minister suggests. I do not want to take up too much of the time of the committee. I know the hon. member for Weyburn wants to ask a question. But I ask the government to give more consideration to the proposal which was put forward seriously a year ago and which is much more than a theory. Many people believe it would make available a great deal of accommodation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is anybody building new homes for the purpose of renting rooms?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, not new homes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But old homes where the occupants do not need all the rooms today. That is what we are referring to in the case of shared accommodation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think it is generally recognized that, while there is a lack of housing accommodation, there must be some measure of rent control. We have had figures given to us this afternoon to indicate that housing construction is not keeping abreast of the demand for houses in this country. As long as a
shortage of housing prevails, we shall have to have some measures passed by this parliament to control the situation. I realize that there are objections to this rent control measure on the part of landlords and also on the part of some tenants. But despite those objections,
I fear what might happen if these controls were abolished at this time. If we are to witness with regard to housing accommodation what has happened with respect to rents of some business premises, it would be a serious situation. We might even face the situation where rent would go up to double and treble what they are now, unless there was some measure to control them. This would cause much more hardship than the present regulations are causing either to the tenant or to the landlord. However, it seems to me that some instructions to favour the tenant must have been given to the commissioners. I should like to ask the question whether or not a directive has been issued to the commissioners to give the benefit of the doubt to the tenant rather than the landlord.
When I say that, I do not wish to be misunderstood. I have had a great number of people who own property write to me. These include old folks and veterans; and the letters seem to indicate that, although they have shown great need, the tenant seems to get every consideration and they do not receive any, despite the arguments they may present. Has any directive been issued which seems to favour the tenant, when these cases come up for consideration?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am sure I cannot answer that question with a positive yes or no. I am quite confident, however, that the answer would be, no. However I would have to check that with the rentals controls officers, before I could answer definitely.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would the parliamentary-assistant endeavour to give an answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, I shall endeavour to>
get a definite answer.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
To turn to another phase of the regulations for a moment,' it is my understanding that the commercial rentals covered by this section ended on March 9. The hon. member for Nanaimo has placed in my hands a communication which brings up a subject with which I think we must deal. . This letter has to to with a small company which occupied commercial space for which it paid $25 a month rental. Now, with the rental order off, notice has been served on this business that from this time forward its rental will be $125 a month, or an increase of 500 per cent.
Transitional Measures Act

Section 6 of order P.C. 9029 reads, in part, as follows:
No person on behalf of himself or any other person shall let or offer to let any real property at a rental that is higher than is reasonable and just or shall charge, demand, receive or collect or pay such a rental . . .
I believe I have seen a press release to the effect that, despite the fact that commercial rentals controls were completely and absolutely off, that clause in the rentals order would be invoked against a landlord with commercial accommodation who proceeded to charge rentals which were not reasonable and just. Would the minister explain what the effect of this is and where it leaves tenants who are occupying commercial accommodation at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The Minister of Finance made a statement on this point in the house on March 5, as reported at page 1908 of Hansard. The hon. member may look at that statement himself, but my recollection is that the effect of it was that the section he has just read is to remain. It is open to the tenant in that event to lay an information, if he wishes, or to report the case for investigation and for prosecution, if it is thought that the facts would warrant such proceedings being taken.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I cannot clearly understand the mechanics of the order. It is not clear to me how the commercial order can be completely and absolutely out of operation-cancelled, so to speak-and yet this section remain, when it applies to a phase of the rentals order which has been cancelled. That is my first thought.
My second thought is that the tenant gets very little comfort from the fact that a prosecution can be laid because, in the meantime, he may have failed to comply with the demand of his landlord and may have been served with a notice to get out. Under those circumstances he would have to vacate, and it would be small comfort to him to know that the rental should have remained at $25 a month when, as a matter of fact, he is out on the street. It seems to me that if, on behalf of the people of Canada, the Minister of Finance desires to see that no wrong is done, before we have finished with this rentals order some amendment should be made which would cover the matter of protection of a commercial tenant in like circumstances.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to return to a point I brought up last night; that is, if the minister is not going to answer the hon. member for Parkdale.
{Mr. Timmins.]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I did not understand that he wanted an answer.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The thing seems incongruous in that apparently the section will be wiped out, so far as commercial rentals are concerned. In view of the fact that commercial rentals are no longer under control, does the minister tell the committee that the present rentals order will protect commercial tenants who are being charged exorbitant rentals?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It applies to the tenant; it applies to the landlord who is charging a tenant a rental which is greater than could be considered reasonable and just. This matter was dealt with by the Minister of Finance when he said:
As the government is continuing rental control on housing accommodation, it is necessary that this section remain in effect.
This section has general application; accordingly, it remains an offence for a landlord to charge a rental for commercial space that is clearly unreasonable and unjust. Should any such case be brought to the attention of the wartime prices and trade board, investigation will be made.
Then he goes on to say that prosecutions cannot be instituted without the leave of the board or of the attorney general of a province. That is found in section 8 of the regulations.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister tell us whether the Minister of Finance intends to implement section 6 any further in favour of a tenant of commercial accommodation who, now that the commercial rentals order is not operative, is left without an anchor, so to speak, so far as protection is concerned? After all, a prosecution would not help that tenant very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance said this in answer to a somewhat similar question:
I believe I can answer that in this way, that if it is clearly established that a rental which is unreasonable and unjust is being charged the board would consider taking a prosecution. It is open under the section for anyone to do it, with the consent of the board or with the consent of a provincial attorney general. I am not prepared to say now to what extent the board should be or would be prepared to undertake the task of prosecutions. What I have said, in effect, is that if cases of that kind are brought to the attention of the board, investigations will be made.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to refer to the questions I asked last night with regard to the rooming-house operators who submitted a brief to the Minister of Finance in which they asked two things. First, they asked that the increased rentals permitted to property owners be extended to cover rentals charged by rooming-house operators. Second, they asked that some relief be given from the six months' freezing order for tenants. I should like to have an answer from the minister.

speechtext: The control on rooming houses came in much later than the regular freezing order. maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The prices of everything involved in keeping a rooming house have gone up since 1943. A government-owned hotel like the Chateau Laurier, which is operated by the Canadian National, is permitted to raise its rates 33i per cent, while a rooming-house operator must stick to the prices he charged in 1943. maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How is it intended to take off these freezing controls? Will it be done by degrees or suddenly? I think it would be better to do it by degrees.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I thought I answered that before. The six months' regulation is applicable unless the tenant is not desirable, in which case he can be evicted under the laws of the province.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There has been a considerable amount of criticism in connection with this housing program and, I think, rightly so. I think everyone will agree that the plan adopted has been absolutely wrong. A landlord who had rented at a low rent found that his rent was frozen at that figure, whereas another landlord might be getting more for the same kind of accommodation. That was all wrong. There should have been an over-all plan whereby rents were brought up to a certain standard. This has caused considerable dissatisfaction. Another cause of dissatisfaction is the fact that a tenant might sublet and obtain more rent than he was paying to the landlord. I think the ones who framed the regulations must take the blame for that.
In certain instances labour is being let out by industry. During the war years many men left the farm to take jobs in war plants and the result was that many farms became idle. Those farms are still idle. When industry is laying off men an effort should be made to find1 out where they came from. If they came from the farm an effort should be made to persuade them to go back to the farm. We are short of labour in the country. You cannot hold floating labour because, as soon as you have a hard job on. your hands, they wall leave you. An effort should be made to persuade these fellows to go out to the farm and occupy some of the houses that are vacant in the country. I doubt if there is a mile and a quarter anywhere in the country without two or three vacant houses. If these men could be persuaded- to go out there it would relieve the housing shortage in the cities as well as the labour problem in the country.
