speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
He asked three questions about these controls. First, had there been a reduction in the personnel engaged in administering the controls, and if so, how much of a reduction, and had some personnel been transferred to other departments of government? There was another question allied to that.
The main departments engaged in the administration of controls were the war departments now being consolidated or liquidated. We can include or not include the defence departments. During the war the defence departments were carrying on certain types of controls. I do not know whether the type of department contemplated by my hon. friend includes the defence departments, but I will give the figures affecting the war departments now being consolidated or liquidated.
The war peak of personnel in the defence departments, civilian employees, was 68,376, which has been reduced as of December 31, 1947, to 14,492. In national war services the war peak was 2,041. That department has been abolished and therefore has no employees. The war peak in the wartime prices and trade board was 5,726, which was reduced as of December 31, 1947, to 1,129. The war peak in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply was 14,540, and that number has been reduced as of December 31, 1947, to 318.
In addition to the departments I have mentioned, the Department of Labour had a great increase in personnel as a result of war activities, especially when wage control was in operation. The war peak in the Department of Labour was 2,813, which was reduced as of December 31, 1947, to 649. The war peak for the unemployment insurance commission was 10,185, which was reduced as of December 31, 1947, to 7,041.
There is one other department that perhaps should be mentioned. With the great growth in the number of employees in the government service during the war there had to be a corresponding growth in the staff of the comptroller of the treasury, whose officers are distributed through all the departments of government. The war peak of employment there was 9,350, which has been reduced to 4,577 as of December 31, 1947. The hon. gentleman asked what has happened to these people, whether they have just been placed in other departments of government. It is impossible to give any definite answer, or anything in the way of figures in reply to that inquiry. For instance, in the wartime prices and trade board there has been movement both ways. Some of those who left the wartime prices and trade board have obtained positions in other departments, and there has been some movement also from other departments to the staff of the wartime prices and trade board. But I am told that, as nearly as can be estimated, the number of persons in the civil service reached a wartime peak of about 142,000; that is, peaks were reached in the various departments at various times, but the wartime peak was about 142,000, and a comparable figure today is 117,232. That information is the nearest to an answer that I can give to my hon. friend.
When I speak about the civil service I want to make it clear that the figures I have given do not include casual employees paid by the hour, do not include revenue postmasters and do not include crown companies personnel. It has been impossible to get the figures for the crown companies personnel in time to give this answer. It might be possible after considerable investigation; I do not know. When I spoke to my hon. friend the other day he said to do the best I could to get that information for him, and I told him that I would.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I thank the minister very much for that information. I am sure that he has been labouring to get it, but, as he says himself, it is still vague. During the war there were two kinds of estimates; there were the ordinary estimates which mentioned all departments, and there were also the special votes which mentioned all departments in order to show that each department was con-
Transitional Measures Act

tributing in some manner to the war effort. It is the same thing with regard to special orders. There are several orders for each department, departments that would not need any special orders at all. For instance, we have them for the Department of Justice. What is the need for the Department of Justice to have a special order? I do not complain about it on account of what the minister has done himself. He was not then Minister of Justice. But why should the Minister of Justice have anything to do with controls, when the Department of Justice is supposed to be managed under the act concerning the Department of Justice?
At the present time my hon. friend is doing his best to answer my question and I thank him for that. But there is the treasury board; there is the civil service commission, these institutions that are supposed to check the movement of the civil service. If I ask today as a member of parliament, what is the composition of the staff of any department today compared with what it was one year ago, two years ago, three years ago, four years ago, five years ago, there should be an answer ready. How many times did I complain that the civil service commission, that the treasury board did not know how to work. Perhaps they have too much to do; but when it comes to elementary things like that, simple figures that all members of parliament have a right to know, how is it that it is so difficult to get them? There is something wrong somewhere. They do not know how to work. They should be taught what to do.
I remember the time that I presided over the civil service committee. I had to tell these people what to do. They were totally ignorant. And w'hen I showed them a chart I asked them if it was all right. They said, "Yes, it is all right." But I said, "What is the thing that is up at the top? Should it not be down at the bottom?" They said, "Yes, sir." And I said, "The other thing that is in this position on the chart, should it not be somewhere else on the chart?" They said, "Yes, sir." I then said to them, "Do your work properly, or do not come before the committee. I want it to be done right now." They said, "It is impossible, sir; we cannot do it." I said, "How is it when I ask you for elementary information, for essential information, you cannot give it to me? Give it to me tomorrow morning at ten o'clock without fail." They said, "Sir, it is impossible." I said, "Tomorrow afternoon at two o'clock without fail." They said, "Oh, sir, you do not know what an amount of work is involved." Then I

said, "This is my last word, the day after tomorrow at ten o'clock without fail." They said, "We will do our best, sir." They came to me and said, "It is not right? Is that not the way it should be done?" They were just children. I will tell the minister that before Mr. Taylor came the wartime prices and trade board was in a completely chaotic condition. It was impossible to deal with them. Those who were running the whole show were trying to show their superiority over members of parliament. They were just stupid asses, and I hope that Mr. Taylor will be able to do something about the other. I wish him well. I hope that he will succeed in doing something with the other people there, and clean the whole house. That is my wish.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: We now com'' fo the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, P.C. 1609 which has to do with construction materials regulations, as amended.

speechtext:
I understand that since last year a new controller has been appointed in respect of priorities or in respect of timber and steel. Is that so? What is the name of the controller? I am told of a case in Toronto where a wholesale hardware merchant received a large quantity of nails which were needed by some 450 builders in that city. That pile of nails was brought in and divided into two parts. One part went to wartime housing and the other part had to be divided between all the other builders in Toronto who, through their local merchants, were to get a share of the nails.
I have a newspaper clipping which was taken from a veterans' paper, a copy of which was received by us all last fall. I notice the heading reads, "Priorities aid Edmonton vets build homes". One item in respect of that hope which I think concerns the committee, mentions material enroute; two carloads of nails, 4,000 kegs. Four thousand kegs are a lot of nails. I should like the minister to tell the committee how this system of priorities is being worked out at the present time and on what basis these priorities of materials are being given to the builders of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The application of priorities is not extensive. The. proportion of nails going into priority projects is about fifteen per cent. In other words, fifteen per cent of nail production goes to priority projects and eighty-five per Cent into free distribution. Priorities apply to low-cost housing and to veteran projects generally. Those are the only priorities that are involved.

Transitional Measures Act

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Are there any priorities now in connection with steel or lumber used for the construction of such things as bridges, and so on by municipalities?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes. There are priorities for steel. All steel is manufactured under allocation. The government approves the rolling schedule for each quarter. The steel requirements are examined! and the steel is allocated as fairly as possible among a great number of users. By careful allocation it is possible to give sufficient steel to all manufacturers, so that their needs can be scheduled at a rate that the industry can support. Every pound of steel made in Canada is subject to allocation by the government, As to lumber, there is no allocation. Lumber is in free supply and can be purchased readily. The only control is in respect of exports.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That applies also to construction timber as well as lumber.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I want to ask a question in regard to the allocation of steel, reverting to the explanation which the minister gave in connection with Bill No. 3 when we were considering that matter. The minister then explained the various projects which came to him, and; when he was discussing those I took it that they referred more or less to rather large individual undertakings. What I am not quite clear about is the situation when you come to smaller things. Is there an allotment of steel in connection with small houses; because in modern houses of this type there are now steel beams? How is the allotment made when you come to small undertakings of that kind? Is the housing corporation allotted so much and does it make a sub-allocation, or how is it done?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend is confusing the import regulations which we were discussing on another occasion with the allocation of domestic steel.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But would this not cover both.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
To an extent. Imports of steel are not controlled in the same way as is the allocation of domestic steel. In other words, if approval is given to a project which requires imports of steel, imports are allowed to come in for that project. But we manufacture about 3,000,000 tons of steel in Canada and that steel is allocated very carefully to a great number of projects. For instance, the automobile industry is allocated so many tons, the shipbuilding industry so many tons a month, each individual shipyard receiving so many tons; the Massey-Harris and' other farm
implement manufacturing concerns are allocated so much; the car building program is allocated so many tons, and so on. Every pound of steel that can be manufactured is allocated to someone. The small man to whom my hon. friend refers buys through jobbers, who are allocated a certain amount, the jobber's allocation being intended to cover the small user.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: When you have household construction competing with other kinds of construction, and particularly having regard to what we have heard about the dearth of household construction, may I ask whether steel is actually a bottleneck in household construction or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The only types of steel that go into household construction are nails and soil pipe.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And I-beams.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I-beams for low-cost housing are not used to any great extent, For houses that sell at $5,000 or $6,000 there are not many I-beams, but larger houses do use a certain amount of structural steel. For a time, soil pipe was a bottleneck and it is still a difficult item. We could get more soil pipe if we could allocate more pigiron to its manufacture, but we have the situation in balance to an extent that it is not a source of handicap in the building of small homes.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wish to ask the minister a series of short questions. Soil pipe is still under the control of this particular order?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, as it applies to priority building and as it applies to the control of steel. The amount of soil pipe that can be made depends upon the allocation of pigiron to the foundries making soil pipe, so that to that extent the amount of soil pipe made is regulated by the distribution of pigiron. But after the soil pipe is made the only priorities apply to soil pipe for priority projects.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: So that the only competition is between private builders and priority projects as far as soil pipe is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: With respect to bricks, is there any control for the manufacture and distribution of bricks at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Practically none. If there is a low-cost housing project that requires brick, at times the co-ordinator of controls will requisition from a brickyard the brick required, but that is a trifling item. Generally
Transitional Measures Act

speaking, there is an ample supply of brick for all purposes and, to the best of my knowledge, no requisitioning is required at the present time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister explain the situation with respect to priorities in plumbing and heating supplies?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In plumbing supplies, production is up 50 or 60 per cent. It is not a serious item at the moment. Orders are placed by Wartime Housing, and sometimes assistance is given to integrated housing contractors who schedule their requirements to meet the program of building for veterans. But generally speaking, plumbing is in fairly adequate supply. The shortage is not in plumbing fixtures, but in plumbers.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is there not still a considerable shortage in bathtubs? Is it not part of the business of priorities in this order to speed up the manufacture of bathtubs, as was done during the war in certain respects, by allocating a given amount of steel to the concerns manufacturing?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Some two years ago steps were taken to encourage the expansion of manufacturing facilities for bathtubs and the desired production was obtained. I believe the bathtubs made today are about 190 per cent of those made in 1945. Demand and supply are pretty well balanced as far as bathtubs are concerned. There is no bottleneck there that I have heard of.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Last year the minister made a statement with respect to the production of nails. I understand from builders that at the present moment nails are in fair supply. The builders are getting by, but they do not know what the situation will be in the month of May when they expect building production, particularly in the residential areas, will be more greatly expanded. Can the minister give a statement as to what we may expect in the way of the production of nails in the months to come?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Production of nails has gone forward rapidly. It is easily 50 per cent over production at the end of the war, but we have really never caught up from the strike situation in 1946. Nails are still in short supply. But as I say, that is not because of any government priority. Government priorities account for about fifteen per cent of total production. We are not far out of balance, but the drop in production of wire rod during the strike has created a vacuum which we have not been able to fill completely.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can the minister give the committee figures as to what percentage of our production of lumber is allocated for export and how that is broken down for individual producers?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes. It is a rather complicated schedule. I will give it to my hon. friend if he is interested.
For eastern Canada, east of the Ontario-Manitoba boundary:
Softwood lumber and sawn softwood railway ties. Exports equivalent to 100 per cent of shipments for Canadian consumption. In other words, the division there is half for domestic, half for export.
Shingles. One car export for each car shipped for Canadian consumption. That is the same thing.
Lath. One oar export for each five cars shipped for Canadian consumption. In other words, with regard to lath we permit the export of only one-sixth of our production.
Poles and piling. Pine poles of any length, and cedar poles between 25 feet and 50 feet in length-one car export for each car shipped for Canadian consumption.
No exports are permitted covering the following items: sawlogs, hardwood flooring, sash, doors and other millwork:
In addition to the before-mentioned export regulations, a free export quota of 290 million feet of softwood lumber for shipment to world markets has been allocated to shippers in eastern Canada, the greater portion of which will originate in the maritime provinces and the Gaspe peninsula. I might say that the reason for the free export quota is that rail hauls to market are costly. There are no rail connections in the Gaspe area, and the rail haul from the maritimes is an expensive item. Since there was not a market for the full 50 per cent allocated to the domestic market in the martime provinces, a free export was given to take up the lumber that could not be used locally.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Has the minister given the figures in connection with softwood ties?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Fifty-fifty.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What about hardwood ties?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Hardwood ties are on fairly free export. We make special arrangements with regard to hardwood ties. I have not them here. We require the martime provinces to fill the railway market demand in that area, and allow export of the remainder. Export quantity depends on the size of the cut. We

Transitional Measures Act
find out how many ties the railroads require for a season; we reserve those ties and allow the balance to be exported.
For Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and *northern and southern interior of British 'Columbia:
Softwood lumber and railway switch ties. Exports equivalent to 100 per cent of shipments for Canadian consumption. In other words, half and half.
Cedar poles 25 feet to 50 feet in length. Two *cars export for each car shipped for Canadian consumption.
No exports are allowed of lath, hardwood flooring, sash, doors and other millwork.
For the Vancouver forest district, which is the British Columbia coastal area and Vancouver island:
Softwood lumber and railway ties. Sixty per cent of production may be exported.
Poles and piling, cedar poles up to 50 feet in length. Two cars export for each car [DOT]shipped for Canadian consumption.
Plywood. Fifty per cent of production may be exported.
No exports on the following items are permitted:
"D" clear and better fir and/or hemlock and/or Sitka spruce in excess of 10 per cent of the shipper's total export shipments, but without limitation as to quantity in individual cars.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No, evidently not. As I was saying, no exports of the following items are
permitted:
"D" clear and better fir and/or hemlock and/or Sitka spruce in excess of 10 per cent of the shipper's total export shipments, but without limitation as to quantity in individual cars.
"D" and better clear flooring, edge, angle and/or flat grain in species other than cedar.
Doors, sash, millwork, railway car material and fir lath.
A priority reserve of 10 per cent of lumber produced is set up to ensure that adequate supplies are provided in Canada for the following users and end uses:
1.	The Canadian railways. Maintenance, repair and new car construction.
2.	Governmental projects, both dominion and provincial.
3.	Mines.
4.	Power projects.
5.	Shipyards.
6.	The manufacture of doors and millwork of all kinds.
7.	The maintenance and repair of saw mills and logging camps, facilities and equipment.
An allocation of 100 million feet of fir, hemlock and balsam logs has been allowed for shipment to the United States during 1948, divided as follows: 17,500,000 feet of Douglas fir; 82,500,000 feet of hemlock and balsam.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the basis of allocation to the producers in each area on the same percentage? That is, does each producer in a certain area receive the same percentage allocation for export and domestic sale?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that there is one car of poles exported to one car sold internally?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Am I correct in saying that steel is not holding back domestic construction? What is the scrap situation? What is the level of our steel production at the moment throughout Canada? Is it in any way retarded by shortage of scrap, and what is the general scrap situation?
Transitional Measures Act

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The steel situation is not limited by scrap, although scrap is a constant worry. We have an embargo on the export of scrap, and we have a substantial import of scrap from countries such as Cuba, and those countries in the Caribbean area. We brought some of the Pearl Harbor scrap in from Manila. Our steel industry is buying scrap w'herever it can be found in the world. But so far shortage of scrap has not limited production. The scrap situation was somewhat relieved by Algoma adopting a duplexing process. In other words, Algoma had an unused Bessemer furnace there, and can make what one might call synthetic scrap from ore, which has taken the Algoma Steel Corporation out of the scrap market and relieved the situation materially. But there is a scrap shortage in Canada as in other countries at the present time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is, I suppose, an enormous amount of metal lying around all over Europe. Is that a practical question, or has any practical means been devised of salvaging and using that metal?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We have not been successful in getting any allocation of that material. I understand that the United Kingdom steel manufacturers are getting a fair amount of scrap from Germany. German cities look like one great mass of twisted structural steel. That scrap is expensive to recover; and France and Belgium are reluctant to let any of it go out of the country. Of course they realize the value of scrap as we do, and they want to save it for their own purposes. England is getting a fair amount out of Germany, and I am not sure whether the Americans are getting some from there, or not. In any event it is not cheap scrap.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister explain to us why it is a necessity to have a steel controller in Canada, as well as the minister's own function as controller and allocator of steel, as Minister of Trade and Commerce, under this new bill we mow have before us?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The steel controller's branch is large. It has assumed the responsibility for directing every bit of steel in this country from its primary stage to finished products. If we were not to do so, the production of steel in this country would drop at least 20 per cent. In other words, the government buys steel from Sydney, Nova Scotia, and brings it to Hamilton, where there is surplus finishing capacity. It buys steel from Sault Ste. Marie, and brings it to Hamilton. It moves pigiron into locations where it would not possibly move

naturally. It helps to move scrap from impossible locations to keep our steel furnaces going.
We have subsidized the steel industry to the extent of three or four millions of dollars, or perhaps more, and this is all handled under the direction of the steel controller. By careful allocation we have been able to keep steel prices in line. The price of basic steel in Canada is lower than the price of basic steel in Pittsburgh, which is a very favourable condition for our secondary manufacturing industries, and one which could be brought about only by the assistance of the government in making the best possible use of our limited basic steel production.

speechtext: Carried.

speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were dealing with the orders concerning the Department of Reconstruction and Supply.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am not going to be critical of the minister this evening, because I know he has carried* a terrific load, not only in connection with his own work but because of what has been placed on his shoulders by other departments. Perhaps it has been impossible for him to do what one might expect should* have been done. I should like to know how the production of houses in Canada compares with production in England. This morning I cut out a clipping which referred to what has been done in England under Mr. Bevan, who apparently has to do with the production of houses. It states that last year they constructed 300,000 new houses. I do not know whether those houses would cost as much as a similar house erected in Canada. I hardly think the house there would be as substantially built, and* perhaps the cost would not be as high. The article states that they have completed two-thirds of their 750,000 house program.
I keep asking myself how they can do that when they have to import at least any lumber or flooring or things of that kind which would be required. I ask myself whether we have done all that could have been d'one here. The minister may tell me that he has, and I am not going to contradict him because I do not know what he has been up against. If we

Transitional Measures Act
have not done all that we should have done, what has been the bottleneck that has prevented us from achieving our objective? The fact is that there is still a great shortage of houses in this country and, if any country in the world should be able to build houses, it is Canada. I realize that labour is one problem.
I have always had the highest regard) for the minister and I had hoped that he would pioneer or suggest some rapid way of building houses. I know that for some time engineers have been developing and promoting steelncore houses which, it is claimed, can be built rapidly. Perhaps the minister would know about that. I should like to have the minister tell us how his program is getting along. If it has been held up, what is the reason? What plans has he now for having hundreds of thousands of new houses built? I presume that many are required.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We have been building houses. We built about 50,000 in 1945; 67,000 in 1916 and about 77,000 in 1947. We have not set our target for 1948 because we are examining the situation to determine how many. Seventy-seven thousand is far more than were ever built in any single year of the history of this country, and the same is true of the 67,000 figure. We have built about 200,000 since the end of the war, and last year we had a carryover, the largest we ever had, of about 45,000 houses in process of construction.
My hon. friend asks how our program compares with that in England. We usually think of England on the terms of four to one. If they have built 300,000, which I may say the available statistics do not indicate they have-[DOT] I would say the figure is much too high-on a four to one basis we are still a little ahead of them. On a population basis Canada compares favourably with any other country in the world in the number of houses built. Sweden was doing better in the immediate post-war days, but they had a slump last year and our three-year total is much better than theirs.	.
My hon. friend suggests that we should invent something new in the way of housing, something better and cheaper. Unfortunately we have the psychology of the tenant to consider. In the early days of the war we were ready to produce a prefabricated house of aluminum, a very comfortable house, but people just would not have them in their towns and the people who lived in them did not like them. That has been the history of prefabricated houses that did not follow conventional styles of architecture.
I was interested in a competition that was held in Los Angeles when I was there a year or so ago. One of the large automobile companies was asked to go into the production of aluminum prefabricated houses. They worked out a design which seemed most attractive, a design that seemed to suit California very well indeed. Before starting into production they built three houses. One was the prefabricated house they intended to build; another was a Cape Cod cottage, and the third was a Colonial style house. All three houses cost about the same and had about the same dimensions. The vote in Los Angeles gave 85 votes out of 100 in favour of the Cape Cod cottage. Their vote showed that people like to live in the type of house in which their ancestors lived and in which they were born. That is one of the difficulties of striking out into new and original patterns of houses.
The material situation is no longer the bottleneck; the bottleneck today is skilled mechanics. We have a housing project in Ottawa of about 450 units. The first units are occupied, but I am told that it will be the end1 of 1948 before sufficient bricklayers and plumbers can be assembled to finish the job. That indicates the shortage of those two trades.
Manpower is the real bottleneck in housebuilding today, particularly skilled trade. We are making some progress as we are getting a few more mechanics every year. The supply situation is in better shape. We are amending the housing act as we go along to overcome difficulties, financial or otherwise, that arise from higher building costs. We are doing the best we can to attain our objectives, and the fact that we have done so in spite of all obstacles is an indication that the housing section is very active indeed.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Has the minister not been very much disturbed at the cost of these structures, and does he see any real sign of a drop in costs? Even leaving out the fantastic instances one hears of occasionally, it seems to me that the ruling costs on these dwellings impose a burden we never would have thought was proper or possible to be carried, whether by owners or tenants. Does the minister feel that there is any real prospect of costs coming down?
Mr. HOWE; One can only speculate. Costs have been levelling off recently. The additional higher labour cost is off-setting greater efficiency in the assembly of materials, but I would say that costs of the type of housing the government builds should not be greater in 1948 than in 1947. It may be a trifle less.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the committee took recess at six o'clock we had agreed to make a statement on the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Limited and on the Canadian Sugar Stabilization Corporation Limited and, with your permission, I am prepared to make them now.
The Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Limited was incorporated by letters patent dated December 24, 1941, as a private company under part I of the Companies Act, 1934. All the shares of the company, other than the qualifying shares of the directors, are heM by the Minister of Finance.
The function of the corporation was and is to pay subsidies and to engage in bulk purchasing of essential Canadian requirements.
Its present activities are as follows:
1.	The only remaining bulk purchasing is the acquisition of Canadian requirements of *"off-shore" oils and fats. Oils and fats are still under international allocation through the international emergency food council, and to a very large extent allocations to Canada have to be purchased from or through the governments in the supplying countries.
2.	The only subsidies still being paid are those on oils and fats.
3.	A large part of the corporation's present activities consists of the liquidation of remaining inventories of antimony and tin, which will soon be completed, and in the checking and closing up of past subsidy accounts. All subsidies paid by the corporation were paid as accountable advances and to most subsidies certain terms and conditions were attached. It is the duty of the corporation to examine the accounts of the recipients of these payments, and in many cases final settlements cannot be concluded until after the close of the last fiscal year of the recipient in which subsidy was paid.
The estimates for the corporation in the fiscal year 1947-48 amounted to forty millions and the estimates tabled for 1948-49 amounted to eighteen millions.
The statement on the Canadian Sugar Stabilization Corporation Limited is very brief. In fact both these statements are necessarily brief because of the lack of time, but if the hon. member wants any further information we shall be glad to get it for him, and there will also be an opportunity on the [DOT]estimates to get the further information required.
The Canadian Sugar Stabilization Corporation Limited was incorporated in March, 1947, for the purpose of taking over the former

functions of the sugar administrator in bulk purchasing of imported cane sugar and Barbados molasses. The Canadian Sugar Stabilization Corporation has acquired or is acquiring Canada's 1948 requirements of imported cane sugar.
The government of Canada has an agreement with the government of the United Kingdom which gives Canada the option of joining with the government of the United Kingdom in purchasing the entire exportable surplus of empire raw cane sugar in 1949.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What effect will that have on the domestic production of non-cane sugar?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not think it has any bearing on that. It is only an option to purchase what we require. The production of beet sugar will certainly be taken care of by this department before it brings in any cane sugar.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I take it that the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, which was created to meet a temporary situation, will in due course disappear. That being so, what is the full significance of PC. 34/4433-Government Employees Compensation Act extended to Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation. Does that mean that up to now these employees have not been eligible for pension?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
They are temporary
employees' and are not eligible for pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is not a pension act but a compensation act, like the Workmen's Compensation Act.

Transitional Measures Act

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I understand that there is no shortage of sugar at the present time for commercial or domestic use and that no subsidy is being paid. Why is it necessary to carry on the Sugar Stabilization Corporation, and what is the estimate for 1948-49?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is nothing in the estimates for the Sugar Stabilization Corporation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why are we keeping the order in council, then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We entered into a contract to take part of this empire sugar for the 1948-49 season, and this is the agency which imports sugar.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why did you enter into the contract if there is plenty of sugar in the world? As a country are we favouring bulk purchasing of our essential commodities?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not think I can give an accurate narrative of this, but I know, when I-was in the Department of Finance, we were entering into contracts for two or three years ahead, and we were carefully considering whether it was advisable to do so or not. Apparently this is the last of the contracts and it covers the 1948-49 crop.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How many months will elapse before the whole matter is disposed of?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: One cannot give an estimate of the number of months, but it will not be very long. I do not know exactly what is meant by that. I cannot give any estimate, but it is not-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It will not be reviewed for the 1949-50 crop, then? It will expire with the present sugar crop year; is that the understanding?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is not likely, but one cannot say anything about that.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not think the question of the hon. member for Rosedale has been answered satisfactorily. I want to go back to what the parliamentary assistant said. My impression was that he spoke about there being the right to purchase, not an actually firm agreement. I think he used the word "optional," or at any rate we had the right to purchase if we wanted to We need to know whether we are bound by the contract or whether it is merely a right that we have to exercise.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We cannot give the committee the exact quantities of sugar that will be required, but we have an option to purchase all that we shall need, minus what we grow in
Canada. That option is with the British government, and therefore it is thought advisable to keep this corporation intact for that purpose until that necessity no longer exists.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The committee is entitled to some information as to what the government's policies are on the purchase of sugar. We get a continual bombardment of pamphlets from our own beet sugar growers. This particular order in council has to do with cane sugar which we refine in this country. I cannot discover whether or not it is to be government policy to purchase sugar in bulk for Canada from Great Britain or from any pool, or whether there is a pool of which the United States is a member and whether Cuba comes into it. We are entirely at sea as to what the policy of the government is. They have the appropriation of their needs, but we do not know how long this will last. They do not know whether they have an option to get cane sugar elsewhere, or under this-particular pooling arrangement. We are entitled to a little light if the government wishes to take power unto itself to regulate the sugar business of this country by order in council.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We buy what sugar we require. May I say that there is on the order paper, in the name of the hon. member for Eglinton, I think, a question which the minister will be answering in a day or two. The hon. member will likely get a statement much more fully than I can give to the committee at this time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: As I understand it, so long as this order in council remains in force no private Canadian dealer can import sugar. It must be all imported through this corporation. Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is that a desirable situation now, or is it a necessary situation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The officials consider it is necessary at the present time, or else they would not ask for this. I do not want to go any farther than that.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I did not hear the answrer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is considered necessary at the present time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Can the parliamentary assistant say why it is considered necessary, and if he does not consider it necessary, might it not be unwise unless we are to go into the bulk purchasing of commodities forever to shut off the private trade longer than is necessary?
Transitional Measures Act

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have a supplementary question to ask. We are entitled to know whether it is a matter of policy to continue bulk buying only when it is necessary, or whether it is considered desirable in itself. In the case of fats and oils my understanding is-if I am wrong I should like to be corrected now-that there is a real reason for doing it. It is a transaction between government and government; but nothing has been said here to indicate that it is not advisable to have the trade carried out by private importers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not think I can say anything more than that or give any more information. I have not it to give. I have not had the opportunity to discuss it with the minister. I know that he will be making a statement on this very point in the course of a day or two. The matter can be raised then. I would like to leave it at that for the moment. I know it is not satisfactory; I admit it is not.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May this order in council stand over? I do not think we should pass it without that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that holds up the whole act. I was hoping we could get this through.
Mr. COCIvERAM: Let us have the answer.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps the minister or the parliamentary assistant could give us some information with regard to the Canadian Sugar Stabilization Corporation, not so much on the supply or the procurement side, in respect of which we could get further information on another occasion, but so far as distribution is concerned. Does a manufacturer or a user of sugar in this country have to apply to this board for a licence or some permit in order to get his supply? I have noticed that the sugar administrator has an expensive suite of offices in the Royal Bank building in Montreal. I do not know why he should occupy such offices. Is he not the same gentleman who is president of the Industrial Development Bank? What is the arrangement with regard to the supply and distribution of sugar under this order in council?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No licence is required. The corporation bring in the sugar and distribute it to refiners as required, and they load it into their own refineries and pay for the sugar. That is the only operation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The refiners, then, must pay the Sugar Stabilization Corporation for the sugar at a price which is fixed by the corporation itself?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: By the corporation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does the parliamentary assistant happen to know whether that price is above or below the world price of sugar?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not know.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Are we at the present time bound by the agreement to belong to this pool for a certain length of time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is not a pool. It is just an agreement with the British for the buying of the exportable surplus of cane sugar that is grown in the empire.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Are we bound by this agreement for a certain length of time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We are not bound unless we have entered into contracts. I do not know what they are. There is no long contract in connection with this.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not think anyone will suggest that we have been unduly holding up anything. We are ready to facilitate the proceedings, but I certainly do not think we should allow this to go through when the member for Rosedale has asked certain searching and pertinent questions which affect the matter of policy and which have not been answered. I think it would be silly to let the thing go through with the record as it is now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am sorry I have no further information, and if hon. gentlemen insist we shall have to let it go over until tomorrow. That is all W'e can do. Perhaps we had better take the transport items before we do that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the committee to allow these items to stand?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The item before the committee, then, under the transport department is P.C. 2245. Shall this item carry?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I know the minister is busy, but there are a couple of points which I wish to bring up in this connection. Take P.C. 2245, which authorizes the chairman of the board of steamship inspection to relieve any ship from the obligation of complying with peacetime regulations. As the order is outlined, it states that, owing to the exigencies of war and the consequent scarcity of ships, these regulations, which are normally complied with in peacetime, shall be set aside. But the order 133/510, which deals with compensation to seamen whose effects have been

Transitional Measures Act
damaged, has been wiped out. There you have a situation whereby the shipping companies can still carry on, using hulls that would not normally be considered seaworthy, and yet the order in council dealing with war damage to seamen's effects is withdrawn. It is such acts that cause dissatisfaction in the ranks of organized labour. If these acts were remedied we would hear a great deal less of what is known at the present time as the communist menace in this country. This stirs it up.
Again, No. 4306 provides for permission to Canadian registered ships to clear on a voyage with masters, mates or engineers not holding appropriate certificates, as amended by 8995. These two provisions enable ships that are not normally seaworthy or properly manned to go to sea, thus endangering the lives of the crew.
Two or three weeks ago I asked the Minister of Transport whether they had reconsidered their stand with respect to the establishment of a coastguard in the light of the sinking of the Clarksdale Victory off Queen Charlotte islands. The answer was to the effect that the cost factor weighed heavily upon his mind. Since that day, two events have taken place in the same area, having a relationship to this question.
In the little fishing village of Massett at the north end of Queen Charlotte islands, a few miles away from the spot where the Clarksdale Victory sank, a certain person became ill and it was necessary to rush that person to hospital. A call was put in to Canadian Pacific Air Lines for this purpose and the cost of transportation was $252 for the flight to Prince Rupert. Two weeks later there was another emergency of the same kind and, as it was not possible to get the Canadian Pacific Air Lines, a telephone call w'as put in for a United States coastguard plane stationed a few miles farther north. They replied that they would be in Prince Rupert within two hours and they came and conveyed the sick person to hospital. They were asked what the charge would be and they replied, "Charge? There is no charge. This is our job".
Here is the point. The best way I can express my opinion is in the words of the hon. member for Temiscouata: I am humiliated as a Canadian. It is all right to get a helping hand from a friend, but when you put the bite on him too often it is too much. It is about time that we in Canada, with our marine history, built up a merchant marine worthy of the country and aided by the necessary protective services. There are more places than the west coast interested in this matter. The. people of the maritime provinces are as deeply interested in it as the people of British
Columbia, and I say to the Minister of Transport that, instead of having a couple of orders in council dealing with the removal of restrictions on steamship companies, he should pass positive orders for the building up of the marine service.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena, very little of which had1 to do with the two orders in council which are on the list of my colleague the Minister of Justice. Evidently they were an excuse for him to make a speech on the necessity of a coastguard service in this country. If my hon. friend wishes to debate that question at the proper time I shall be glad to hear what he has to say, but this is not the, proper time under these orders.
However, there are two things that seem to bother him, and I shall deal with them. The first is this. He seemed to object strenuously to one of these orders being revoked, namely P.C. 133/510, having to do with compensation to seamen, war damage to effects. The reason that order ini council is being revoked is that it has lapsed. There are no longer any claims under that order in council, and neither are there claims by the dependents of seamen by virtue, of the sections of the order. So* it was thought expedient to revoke it. Had there been any claims or had all the claims not been paid up under this order, the recommendation would have been made to extend it.
The second matter complained of is the order having to do with the relieving of ships from steamship inspection. My hon. friend says he knows of instances where ships have been allowed to ply in an unseaworthy condition.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No. I said this allows them to ply the trade routes in a condition that is not seaworthy according to ordinary peacetime standards.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend reads the order in council carefully he will see that the chairman of the steamship inspection board has the right, subject to the approval of the minister, to grant relief from certain parts of part VII of the Canada Shipping Act, having to do with steamship inspection. But it is clearly set out in the order that on no condition shall he grant that permission to proceed to sea if the ship is in an unseaworthy condition. The chairman of the steamship inspection board has repeatedly told me that on no occasion has he exempted a ship from the provisions of this part of the act when he was satisfied that the ship was in an unseaworthy condition. P.C. 4306, the second order, simply
Transitional Measures Act

relieves the ship from the operations of sections 113 and 114 of the act and sections 132 and 133 in so far as clearances are concerned. Both of these orders in council will be contained in the new amendments to the Canada Shipping Act which I hope to be able to bring down to this house.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
As another deep-sea fisherman, I should like to say a few words on this particular item. I agree with the hon. member for Skeena. We are not so much concerned about the orders that are being retained as we are about the ones that are being wiped out, one of which is P.C. 133/510, with regard to compensation to seamen, war damage to effects and so on. Wartime conditions necessitated the passing of that order. It was presupposed that those sailing ships at that time would be sailing under conditions much more hazardous than and completely different from those which prevailed in peacetime sailing. So the government passed an order to compensate anyone who might run into difficulty because of wartime conditions in shipping. That particular order in council is being , wiped out, but the very orders in council which set up the conditions that necessitated the passing of the previous order are being retained.
Despite the fact that the minister says the inspector can do this or that, on the approval of the minister, it is not what the minister says in this house that counts. I have all the respect in the world for him and his word. He is still boring down there at the strait of Canso. He has been telling me that all the time, and I believe him. But the fact of the matter is that, if it comes to a test, it is not what the minister said in Hansard that counts. It is what this order in council says that counts. I think the first order, the order for compensation that I am talking about, should have been retained if the conditions contained in the next two orders which protect and give a good deal of latitude to the shipping companies are to be retained; because the very conditions that you were trying to guard against there from the point of view of compensation are permissible to the shipping companies. Listen to this-and this is P C 2245:
... to authorize . . . the chairman of the board of steamship inspection to relieve any ship, or the owner of any ship, from the obligation of complying with any of the provisions of part VII of the Canada Shipping Act . . . excepting therefrom those provisions of the said part and regulations made thereunder relating to radio and telegraph installations on ships. . .
And so on. The matter is entirely in the hands of the inspector of shipping. As the hon. member for Skeena pointed out, it does

not make any difference what kind of ship it is. If the inspector says it is quite all right, you can sail. It is no use for someone to protest and say that the minister said in the house, "Well, that does not apply." If it does not apply, it should be wiped out. That particular section of the act which has been set aside afforded protection to the seamen. It guaranteed them that inspectors were obligated to see that certain standards were maintained with regard to ships that left port. All right then.
We come to the next one and it is much worse. Your compensation act was passed because the government visualized and, I think, rightly so, that every ship which could sail would have to be used during the war, that many of them would be in an unseaworthy condition and that sailors would be taking additional risks. So some extraordinary means of compensation was provided. The compensation is now wiped out but the conditions that made it necessary to pass the compensation provision in the first place are-retained.
We now come along to P.C. 4306. This one is worse, but it is still being retained. If, as the minister says, these provisions that I have just been quarrelling with are not applicable, then this ought to be taken off the board also; run a stroke through i-t -and say it is not necessary.
Listen to the next one, P.C. 4306, which is to provide for permission to Canadian registered ships to clear on any voyage with masters, mates or engineers not holding appropriate certificates, as amended by P.C. 8995. What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It provides for permission to clear on a voyage, not on any voyage.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is not any difference. The ship just goes out. That is all.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Consider the poor crew.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If we read that, what does it mean? It means that you are cutting completely your standards for officers and their qualifications, and the guarantee to ordinary seamen that they have competent officers manning that ship when it leaves port. It places in the hands of the shipping companies the privilege and power of discriminating against men who have worked their way up, qualified and, now hold masters' certificates and so forth. That, too, maybe was necessary during the war when there were so many ships at sea, and when personnel was so difficult to obtain. But it is not necessary today, with the maritime service that was built up during the war, and with the large number of men

Transitional Measures Act
who took naval training and qualified at a good deal of expense and trouble to themselves. Men who hold these qualifications will demand adequate compensation for the services they rendered. So we are retaining here an order in council that enables shipping companies to pick up men out of the rank of the unemployed, men who are forced, perhaps through economic pressure, to take employment on ships of this kind, while, at the same time, you leave on the beaches men who are qualified. If this order in Council is not applicable; if it does not mean that; and if it is the intention of the Department of Transport to use personnel built up during the war, men who are qualified and competent, then this should be removed, and the Canada Shipping Act as applied to the trained personnel should be applicable instead of the wartime regulations.
You are removing now an order in council that made compensation applicable to certain personnel who may have run into conditions brought about by the order in council. Are you making any provision to replace that compensation order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No. I told the hon. member for Skeena a moment ago that that order in council P.C. 133/510 has lapsed. No more claims have been made by virtue of it. Therefore it has used itself up. There is no need for carrying it on.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
For instance, a snag boat, Port Essington, ran into difficulty, and the men lost all their effects. This was a government vessel, and they lost all their clothing. There is no law which says that the government was liable for the clothing they lost. A boat of the Canadian National Railways burned up in Ketchikan, Alaska and, in that case, the railway company was not liable for the effects lost, but they did reimburse the men, out of the goodness of their hearts. Now the seafarers' international union wants to see in the Canada Shipping Act an item covering loss of effects, or an order along that line, which would apply in peacetime, so that if a ship is sunk at sea the men will be compensated for the clothes and personal belongings they had with them.
There is no difference between a boat going down in the middle of the Atlantic in peacetime and one going down in wartime. It is just the same thing. The water is cold.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I was just about to finish, but I wish to thank the hon. member for Skeena for helping. I do not think the minister's answer was satisfactory. It was to the effect that when there were no more claims the
order in council should be allowed to lapse. If there were no more claims, so much the better. But why not leave the order in council there? In case of an emergency there may be claims. And, as the hon. member for Skeena has pointed out, a sailor who loses his effects at sea is just as seriously affected as if he had lost them during wartime. If it is not costing anything, except the fact that it is there against the time when something may occur, then it should have been carried forward; if you are going to carry these others forward.
Is there any intention on the part of the minister or his department to provide something along the lines contained in the terms of the order in. council?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The order in council my hon. friend has dealt with is one which was passed under the War Measures Act, and it is explained in the order just what is meant by war damage. Perhaps I had better read it to the hon. member. Paragraph (c) of the regulations defines war damage as-
Loss (including destruction) and damage caused by, or in repelling, enemy action or by measures taken to avoid the consequences of damage caused by or in repelling enemy action.
My answer was based upon, the definition contained in the order in council when I replied to my hon. friend.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I regret I have not order in council 2245 before me, but I should like to ask the minister a question about it. My interpretation of it is that it is retaining certain easements in the selection of certain officers on ships which were removed during the war because of shortage of personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is order in council P.C. 4306; it is not P.C. 2245.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was talking about P.C. 2245. I know the minister has had communications with radio officers from the Pacific coast. They have made representations to him in order that they may have their positions assured. Does the retention of this order mean that radio officers must be carried as heretofore on ships sailing on the Pacific coast?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The best way I can answer that is by saying that this does not affect the position which existed prior to the passing of the order, in so far as radio telegraphers or officers are concerned; that is, the order excepts radio and radiotelegraphy.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Is P.C. 4306 retained because there is still a shortage of qualified men?
Transitional Measures Act

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Quite so; that is the reason for it. I can also tell my hon. friend it is the intention to carry these two orders into the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act.
While I am on my feet, perhaps I might reply to the objection of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. These two orders in council as they now stand on the list of my colleague are today sections of the merchant shipping act of the United Kingdom. That country saw fit to include the terms of these orders and, in fact, to go farther than one of them, in their act. So that I do not think we make any mistake if we follow the precedent created there.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OP CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It will be recalled that orders in council passed in 1943 reserving title to radioactive minerals on crown lands in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon were extended under the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947, largely because the question of ownership of ores in the ground was still under discussion in the united nations atomic energy commission and it was felt that no action should be taken here that might embarrass those discussions. Since then, the second report of the united nations commission has been published, -and that report does not contemplate ownership of ores in the ground by any international authority which may be established. As I told the house on March 25 last, the policy of the government is that radioactive material be controlled after it has been mined and the atomic energy regulations of Canada provide for this sort of control.
While the orders in council were in effect and until the atomic energy regulations had been passed, it was necessary that mining operations be exclusively in the hands of the government. The whole situation has been reviewed in the light of present circumstances and changed conditions, and the government is now satisfied that it is in the best interests of Canada that restrictions against private prospecting and private development of radioactive minerals should be removed and has-accordingly revoked the orders in council' which reserved to the crown title in these minerals in the territories.
The policy decided upon is as follows:
The government will purchase through Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited,

Transitional Measures Act
or other designated agency, acceptable uranium bearing ores and concentrates on the following basis:
1.	A minimum uranium content equivalent to 10 per cent by weight of uranium oxide (U3O8) in the ores or concentrates will normally be required.
2.	Price will be based upon the uranium content of the ores or concentrates and will be at the minimum rate of $2.75 per pound' of contained (UaOg) f.o.b. rail and will be guaranteed for a period of five years.
3.	This price includes all radioactive elements in the ores or concentrates, but consideration will be given to the commercially recoverable value of non-radioactive constituents by adjustment of price or by the redelivery of the residues containing such constituents.
4.	Under special circumstances, consideration may be given to payment of a higher price or to acceptance of ores or concentrates of lower grade.
5.	All operations will be carried on subject to the provisions of the atomic energy regulations of Canada.
That constitutes the new policy. As noted, the new policy permits private exploration and private mining and proposes to encourage both by putting on the ores a definite minimum value, which will be the minimum value for the next five years. I might say that I was interested to note that the semi-annual report of the United' States atomic energy commission to the Senate and the House of Representatives, which reached me only yesterday, contains the following two paragraphs:
The commission believes new reserves of source materials can best be developed by competitive private industry, under the stimulus of profits, and the means of accomplishing this are under study.
In general it will be commission policy to purchase ores for its program from private sources and limit direct government production as far as possible.
It would seem that, although we arrived at the Canadian policy independently, the policy of the United States will follow parallel lines.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while it is true that on Friday evening I moved the adjournment of this debate I feel that, since I had an opportunity to discuss this subject, first on the resolution, and again on the second reading last Friday, I should not take up too much of the time of the house but should allow other hon. members to have their say.
