maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the bill.
As to the first section of it, which provides for the establishment of a pension fund for the employees of the wheat board, I am of the opinion that the farmers will look with favour upon this proposal, provided, of course, that the funds to be taken out of the moneys of the wheat board are reasonable, and I submit that any such deductions from the wheat board funds should be reasonable. In order to ensure that they shall be reasonable, I would suggest to the government that in committee we should add a subsection to this clause to the effect that the advisory committee of the wheat
	|
board should consent to the deductions to be made out of the board's funds. I rather welcome this section because it lends an air of permanency to the wheat board act which it lacks at the present time.
The second section deals with payments to producers. It is under this section that the farmers expect further payments to be made on their 1945, 1946 and 1947 deliveries. It is this part of the bill which is particularly urgent, because the money is so badly needed by the farmers in the west at the present time. I am hoping that these payments will be made as large as possible. In view of the international wheat agreement which has just been concluded and the short supply of food in general, I think the board would be justified in paying out all the moneys which they now hold in trust for the farmers.
I have received numerous letters from farmers in my constituency in connection with these anticipated payments to be made by the wheat board, and I must say that the farmers feel that much more should be paid to them than the rumoured twenty cents. Unless the payment is as generous as possible, there will be great disappointment and great dissatisfaction.
I also think that, when making these payments, the board should send along a brief statement showing the farmer what has happened: to his wheat that he delivered to the board. I should like to read part of a letter which I received from a farmer in my constituency, in order to give the house some idea of what the general feeling is among the farmers. He says, in part:
Sixty-five per cent of the farmers are without seed and feed.
Remember he writes from the northwestern part of my constituency, where he experienced a crop failure last year. He goes on:
Owing to the bad season thousands of them are walking the streets trying to find a dollar to feed wife and' children. Why should the wheat board be allowed to keep this money, and when spring comes farmers have to get down on their knees to managers of chartered banks only to be insulted? The wheat board has to account for three hundred million bushels sold at over $3 a bushel. This is not including what they sold to Britain. There is also a 160,000,000 bushels that the millers subsidized to farmers at 30 cents a bushel. We are asking you to put that before the government and not to accept payment of twenty cents a bushel.
I cannot vouch for the correctness of the figures this farmer gives in his letter, but I am putting the letter before the house to show what the farmers on the prairies are thinking,

Canadian Wheat Board Act
and to urge upon the government the necessity of making the largest possible payment and submitting to the farmer at the same time a brief statement of what has happened to his wheat.
With respect to the last part of the bill, which concerns the marketing of oats and barley, I am really amused by the arguments advanced in this house that the majority of the farmers of western Canada do not favour the handling of coarse grains by the wheat board or by some grain board. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) was undoubtedly the most outspoken proponent on behalf of those who wish to go back to the open market system of marketing grain. While I respect his views, to which he is, of course, entitled, I should like to quote what he said at page 2119 of Hansard:
So I say that with respect to barley and oats . . . there is no majority demand in western Canada for the passing of this legislation.
Again, at page 2124 of Hansard, he says:
So we find ourselves in this position. This measure is not seriously asked for by anyone. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is divided on it; we know that.
The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), as well as the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) and other members from the west have already refuted these arguments and have shown, especially in connection with the resolutions and representations of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, that this body has for the last three years definitely asked for this legislation and has stood on the side of orderly marketing through a grain board. I shall have a little more to say about that later on so far as my own constituency is concerned.
There has been considerable agitation on behalf of the members of the grain exchange in Winnipeg to return to the open market system, and the tactics employed to persuade the farmer to change his mind about this orderly marketing are the same as the arguments employed by my hon. friend the member for Calgary West.
Major Strange, a public relations officer of the Searle Grain Company, one of the big companies doing business in the west, has been particularly active in this respect. In a letter to the editor of Saturday Night, published in an issue of that periodical on March 6, he proposes to show or prove exactly the same thing that the hon. member from Calgary West tried to show the other day, namely, that there is no majority demand in western Canada for the handling of grain, including wheat, by the wheat board.
In this letter Major Strange says in part:
The Searle Grain Company has just published the results of a recent poll which reveals that 76-4 per cent of the farmers are now gravely dissatisfied.
Undoubtedly he refers to an organized campaign by the Searle Grain Company, through their local elevator agents, of circulating among the farmers and presenting to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) a petition asking for higher prices of grain. This petition was circulated among farmers in these points where the Searle Grain Company have elevators. The company was good enough to advise me by letter on December 10, 1947, that petitions had been sent in to them from five points within my constituency. To the letter was attached a copy of a letter to the then minister of trade and commerce, in which they enclosed the petitions, and in this letter they wrote as follows:
So far we have received about half of the replies which we anticipate will come in, and those who are dissatisfied with present prices and wish higher prices represent 79 per cent of the farmers from these points.
I wrote the company asking them to let me have a copy of the petition and also the number of signatures which they had received from the five shipping points in my constituency, and they were good enough to send me a copy of the petition and to advise me of the number of signatures. The petition, it is true, did not ask for a return to the open market, but it was worded in such a manner that its aims could be realized only by returning to the open market system of marketing our grain. The number of signatures in these five shipping points in my constituency were from six to thirty-five and the total was under sixty. This was, of course, a negligible number. I certainly dispute the fact that these represent the opinion of seventy-nine; per cent of the farmers from these points.
I may say that in my constituency I have eighty-five shipping points; therefore these five points that sent in these petitions is a very small number indeed. Since last November; yes, even since last October I have received resolutions from wheat pool committees in at least half of these shipping points, urging that the wheat board should be the sole marketing agency for all grains, which means wheat and all coarse grains. The wheat pool membership in my constituency is 7,136, out of a total population of 32,000. I admit that there are some duplications, and some of these members are not active producers any more, but I think I can safely say, after
Canadian Wheat Board Act

going through my petitions, that ninety per cent of the farmers in my constituency, perhaps more, are members of the wheat pool, and the resolutions which have been sent in to me represent almost the unanimous opinion of these wheat pool members.
Undoubtedly the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) have received copies of these resolutions; in fact, I know they have, and perhaps they have received more than I have. These resolutions, without one exception, ask for the marketing of coarse grains by the wheat board or by some grain board1.
I do not wish to repeat the arguments previously made to support my contention. The stand of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has been mentioned several times. The presentation madle by the hon. member for Rosthern of the feeling of the rural municipalities saves me from quoting from the proceedings of their convention which was held in the last week in February. There is no question that this convention-that is the convention of the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities-is certainly representative of Saskatchewan agriculture. Besides the numerous resolutions, I have received numerous letters from outstanding farmers in my constituency. I should like to quote just one short paragraph from a letter of one who, for decades, has been high in the councils of agriculture. This is what he says:
With particular reference to feed grains being placed under the wheat board, there is no question that the overwhelming majority of western farmers are in favour of this move. Personally I have yet to meet one farmer since October 21 -who is in favour of the futures market for any of their grain.
I should like to place on record the resolution which was passed1 by the Saskatchewan legislature on March 4 last. This resolution was unanimously adapted by the legislature. A division was called and it was passed unanimously, with no vote against it. The Liberal members and the soldiers' representatives voted with the rest of the members of the legislature in favour of this resolution:
That this assembly:
(1) Records its opinion that the removal of marketing controls and the return to the medium of speculative trading in coarse grains has caused uncertainty, hardship and widespread loss to producers of coarse grains and livestock, and that only through the orderly marketing of all grains will producers enjoy the benefits of long-term stable prices, and,

(2) Urges that the dominion government:
(a)	reimburse all producers who marketed their 11147 coarse grains prior to the decontrol order of October 21, 1947, for their losses out of the speculative profits made on their grain-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Order. I must call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that we have before the house second reading of Bill No. 135, to amend the wheat board
act.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I submit that I am entirely in order. I am asking that the bill be adopted and that the farmers are asking for the approval of this act which is now under consideration. Surely I am in order. I continue:
(b)	immediately establish a national marketing board with adequate producer representation, to market all grains in an orderly manner, and
(c)	simultaneously and permanently close the Winnipeg grain exchange.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, there is any argument whatsoever that this move to let the wheat board handle grains exclusively is the wish of the vast majority of the farmers on the prairies. Who else has really anything to say in the matter? Surely it is the farmers' business, and they ask us today that we help them establish orderly marketing which they think is essential for their well-being.
I come to the last part of the amendment which refers to oats and barley. I am sorry that the Minister of Trade and Commerce now talks about necessary complementary legislation as if the proposed section dealing with oats and barley were ultra vires, as the Minister of Agriculture hinted last year it might be. I maintain that the proposed legislation is neither ultra vires, nor does it requir complementaiy legislation on the part of the provinces. No one contends that the act, as it now stands, is ultra vires; and if it is in the powers of parliament to legislate about orderly marketing of wheat in the realm of interprovincial and international trade, why should parliament not have the same powers with respect to oats and barley and any other grain? That is the way the farmer would argue, and, of course, he would be right.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) was asked last year about the constitutionality of the act as we now have it. This is what he said on February 21, 1947, and it can be found in Hansard of that year at pages 839 and 840:
The opinion of the law officers of the crown is that the bill as drafted is within the constitutional powers of the dominion parliament. Naturally that is so; otherwise the government would not have introduced it.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
The bill is the exercise of the power of the dominion parliament to regulate interprovineial and export trade and commerce in wheat produced in designated areas . . . There may be other constitutional bases upon which the legislation can be set, but the main reliance for constitutionality of the legislation is upon the trade and commerce power in section 91 of the British North America Act . . .
It should be understood that the producer will have the option of selling the wheat which he grows either into interprovineial or export markets through the Canadian wheat board or, alternatively, into local markets in the provinces, which he may do himself, not through the Canadian wheat board.
The quota control is based upon our jurisdiction over elevators and mills designated as for the general advantage of Canada, and over railways.
That concludes the quotation from the Minister of Justice, and I may say with that I fully agree. I have no doubt that this opinion is based upon the law propounded in the reference re the Natural Products Marketing Act, 1934, case. The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada is reported in 1936, 3 D.L.R., 622, and the judgment of the privy council upholding the Supreme Court of Canada is contained in 1937, 1 D.L.R., 691. The result of the decisions was that the act was held to be ultra vires because, in the language of the Chief Justice of Canada, Sir Lyman P. Duff, contained on page 644 of the report:
The powers of regulation vested in the commissions extend to external trade and matters connected therewith and to trade in matters of interprovineial concern, but also to trade which is entirely local and of purely local concern.
In other words, the act was held to be ultra vires because it concerned trade within the province itself, while, of course, this act concerns itself only with interprovineial and external trade. I think it would be well to quote a further paragraph from this famous judgment in order to make it absolutely clear that the wheat board act as it now stands, and as it is proposed to be amended, is fully within the competence of parliament. The chief justice quotes from the Parson's case on page 625:
Construing therefore the words "regulation of trade and commerce" by the various aids to their interpretation above suggested, they would include political arrangements in regard to trade requiring the sanction of parliament, regulation of trade in matters of interprovineial concern, and it may be that they would include general regulations of trade affecting the whole dominion.
And again, on page 626:
Here again there is no suggestion that trade in a particular commodity, in so far as it is 5849-146J
external trade or interprovineial trade, is not within the exclusive regulative authority of the dominion.
After reviewing numerous decisions on the powers of parliament on the subject of trade and commerce, the chief justice says this, at page 629:
It would appear to result from these decisions that the regulation of trade and commerce does embrace the regulation of external trade and the regulation of interprovineial trade and such ancillary legislation as may be necessarily incidental to the exercise of such powers.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question? I do not think anyone disputes the fact that the federal government has complete control of trade crossing interprovincial boundaries, but will my hon. friend explain how the board can control trade within a single province?

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is not proposed in the act. All that is proposed in the legislation that is before us is to have interprovineial and external trade in oats and barley.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: But may I point this out. We have no doubt whatever that the present bill is wholly legal and within the competence of the federal parliament to pass, but the point is that a workable marketing system cannot be based upon that bill, unless the marketing authority can also control marketing within a single province.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I submit that the wheat board act seems to have worked all right in the last twelve months in regard to wheat; and I further suggest that on the same basis, and under the same provisions as are proposed in this bill, the wheat board will also satisfactorily handle the trade in oats and barley in interprovineial and external trade. The act itself says, in subsection 3, of section 2, that the board is incorporated with the object of marketing in an orderly manner, in interprovincial and export trade, grain grown in Canada, and shall possess certain powers. It does not say wheat, but grain in interprovincial and export trade. This section just quoted is contained in Part II. Part II is not being amended, because it deals with all grain and not just wheat; it is only parts III and IV that deal with wheat, and the section I have quoted is taken from part II. We come to part III, which is to be extended' to oats and barley, andi again "the board shall undertake the marketing of wheat produced in the designated area in interprovineial and' export trade," and all that the amendment will do will be to give the board power to undertake the marketing of oats and barley produced
Canadian Wheat Board Act

in the designated area in interprovincial and export trade. Again, in the heading of part IV, it is stated distinctly that it just deals with interprovincial and export trade, and all three sections of part IV deal with nothing but interprovincial and export trade. Part IVA, which is to be added, provides that the governor in council may, by regulation, extend the application of part III or of part IV or of both to oats and barley, and the new part IVA therefore, will effect only transactions in interprovincial and export trade in those two commodities, oats and- barley; and of course it is quite within the jurisdiction of parliament to legislate.
There is one thing which is not quite clear to me. Why should oats and barley transactions be subject to order in council? Why not just say that the board shall undertake the marketing of oats and barley in the designated area in interprovincial and export trade and that parts III and IV shall be made applicable to oats and barley? This is what the farmers want. In fact they want to include all grain. Why leave it to the whim and fancy of the government as to whether or .not oats and barley shall be handled by the wheat board?
Another aspect which I do not like, and about which we shall need an explanation, is this. This amending section says that the government may, by order in council, apply or extend the provisions of part III or IV to oats or barley or to both. In my opinion it should say "and". That is, parts III and IV should apply to oats and barley, because it seems to me that both are necessary, one supplementing the other.

If he cares to look it up he will find that, obviously, I did not say that.
I turn now to the odd remark made by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke).
I suppose there would be no law business if lawyers did not disagree. For the moment I am not going to argue the constitutional aspect of the matter. Indeed, I am relying on exactly the same case to which he had referred.
I shall quote only a few lines from the conclusion of the judgment of Mr. Justice Duff, which apparently the hon. member did not read, or perhaps did not read with his usual care.
This appears in a special edition of the case published by the king's printer in 1937, and contains the text of the act and the judgment of His Lordship Sir Lyman Duff, Chief Justice of Canada, and also the judgment of the privy council. I would read only these few lines from the judgment of Mr. Justice Duff, in closing:
To summarize: in effect, this statute attempts and indeed, professes to regulate in the province of Canada, by the instrumentality of a commission or commissions appointed under the authority of the statute, trade in individual commodities and classes of commodities.
The powers of regulation vested in the commissions extend to external trade and matters connected therewith and to trade in matters of interprovincial concern; but also to trade which is entirely local and of purely local concern.
Regulation of individual trades, or trades in individual commodities in this sweeping fashion, is not competent to the parliament of Canada and such a scheme of regulation is not practicable.
Those are the final and deciding words of His Lordship in that case and, as I say, we are both relying on the same case for the views which we hold.
I want to turn back for a moment and correct a statement in the speech I made on Thursday last. I used a word wrongly and I want to apologize to those to whom it applied. I was interrupted by some hon. member to my left. After I had said that the wheat pools in the west had gone bankrupt, someone interrupted and said that that had happened because they had advanced too much money to the farmers. I then suggested that it was on account of the stupidity of the directors. It was really a mistake in judgment of the directors, and that is what I meant to say.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

However, in the excitement of the exchange I used the word "stupidity", which I had no right whatever to use.
I should like to make a second correction. I was interrupted by another hon. gentleman to my left, I think it was the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), when I was speaking of one Aaron Shapiro who came out west and formed our wheat pools. He suggested that they had asked him to come there and I agreed with him. But I was wrong. Aaron Shapiro came to western Canada and was paid for his trip by the Calgary Herald and the Edmonton Journal. The farmers of Alberta and Saskatchewan had nothing whatever to do with the invitation to that man to come to the country. Those newspapers asked him and they paid his expenses and fees.
I am going to say only a word or two about barley and then I shall sit down. This is -really a governmental- matter and not so much a pool matter. We are well aware of this fact, and I am bringing it out because of the injury that certain policies may do us in the future. There is an embargo on the export of barley to the United States and one can export only under permit. In times gone by, they got a good deal of money from that, because the price of the permit was roughly the difference in the prices prevailing in the two countries. From that they formed an equalization fund which helped in making payments to the grower for the barley so handled.
For some time malting barley sold to maltsters and brewers has commanded a price of $2.50 a bushel-a while ago it was $2-in the middle western United States which are quite close to us. That is the logical market for that product. I know it has become a habit with some people to say that we talk too much about the western farmer and his products. I am anxious to assure the eastern members that we are not down on our knees asking for anything from anybody for the western farmer. We believe he has been the goat in connection with hogs and cattle and everything he grows, whether it be animal or vegetable, ever since these controls came in. As we have so often said, he is still controlled while that which he buys is not controlled.
I give you this simple picture of a bushel of malting barley. It weighs forty-eight pounds and it will make thirty-six pounds of malt. That has been selling for hog feed because, while we had ceilings, there was no distinction in the grades of barley. Everything went at the ceiling price and you got for low-grade barley the same price as you got for malting barley, which, of course, always carries a premium.

What is happening in the middle west United States today is that the maltsters and brewers are conducting an active campaign to have barley grown in their own country for their purposes.
Let us take a bushel of malting barley in Canada. It weighs 48 pounds and it makes thirty-six pounds of malt. The dominion government places a tax of sixteen cents a pound on the malt, so that a return of $5.76 is obtained by way of tax from every bushel of barley which is malted. They believe in getting control, even ownership of the things which we produce and the methods of distribution. That is another argument, for they have a logical position. I know of no member in this house who professes to be opposed to socialism who has a single leg to stand on if he supports orderly marketing as they call it, but what is actually the compulsory grabbing of the farmer's grain. That is not orderly marketing. That is the beginning of the police state, and I hate the word just as much as anyone else does. But you can only compel by penalties. You can only succeed in bringing compulsory schemes into being by penalties. Some may say we have lots of penalties now; we have the criminal code. Yes, and that is enforced by penalties. The only way you can do this thing is by penalties. What does that mean? It would have to be done by force. The end of socialism can only be the operation of the Canadian economy by force, and those of us who disagree with that principle-I admit again, they may argue for it-have not a leg to stand on in this oats and barley business if we vote in favour of this compulsion.

There is a danger that we might lose sight of what is actually involved in the principle of this bill. The principle, as I see it, is whether or not the members of this house believe in stabilization of farm income and in orderly marketing. In spite of all that has been said to my right, when the vote is taken on this measure we shall see where the official opposition stand on this important question. If the hon. member for Calgary West is putting forward the policy of the party to which he belongs it would be logical to see every member of that party vote against this bill. On the other hand, if the policy of that party is as it has been expressed on some occasions by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), then we might expect something different.
So far as we and the people who have sent us here are concerned, we have no doubt where we stand. I have before me a clipping from one of the weekly papers published in my constituency, the Dauphin Herald, which gives a tabulation of where the farmers of the prairie provinces stand on the wheat contract with Britain. It is dated April 24, 1947, almost a year ago. The poll question submitted was this:
The 1946 wheat agreement between Canada and Great Britain sacrifices the opportunity to sell at higher prices now for the assurance of stabilized prices for the next four years. Is this a sound principle?
The question did not refer to the details of the British wheat agreement but to the principle of a stabilized market for the future in preference to taking what you can get now and taking a chance on getting next to nothing in the future. The tabulation shows that seventy-nine per cent of the farmers of the prairie provinces replied, yes; they were in favour of that principle without any reservation; seventeen per cent replied, yes, with reservations, and only two per cent were opposed to that principle. I think that answers for all time the question which has arisen in this debate as to where the farmers of the prairie provinces stand on the question of orderly marketing.
Not long ago it was announced in this house and appeared in the press that an international wheat agreement had been reached, under which three of the nations undertook to sell 500 million bushels of wheat a year and thirty-three other nations undertook to buy
Canadian Wheat Board Act

it at a certain price. It is interesting to note that two of the wheat-producing nations of the world were opposed to entering into this agreement. We hear a great deal these days about the Big Four, the Big Five, and so on, but on that question a sort of Big Four appeared to be emerging. We were told that Soviet Russia and the Argentine were opposed to this international wheat agreement. To complete the Big Four, we have in this country the Winnipeg grain exchange and the Progressive Conservative party.
I believe that we should make our position clear on the principle which is actually involved in this bill. There has been a great deal of talk, much of it coming from the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), as to the intentions of members on the opposite side of the house in connection with the inclusion of oats and barley. We have made our position clear. In fact, last year one of the members of this group moved to have oats and barley included in the bill itself. For example, he was asked in the middle of his speech by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Argue) this question:	Do you believe in price control?
The reply was, No, if you do not control some other matters at the same time. To make sure the matter was sufficiently confused, he added this: Furthermore I do not believe in the attempt to control prices by government edict.

Fannystelle, Manitoba, March 6, 1948.

House of Commons,

After reading your contribution to the Hansard of February 27, I feel that it is my duty to write to you thanking you for your interest in western agriculture.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
Although we have a Canadian Federation of Agriculture and a Canadian wheat board, I cannot see that either of them are in any way interested in our welfare, nor are they in any way obligated to represent our cause, as western agriculture could not claim to hare chosen them.
The three prairie provinces have for some years back supplied all of Canada with wheat for domestic milling, at about half price. About seventy million bushels each year.
The monetary loss is a big one, but it is totally eclipsed by the fact that >we have had taken from us the right to sell our grain, and we are compelled to hand it over to the government who are permitted to sell it where they wish, for a small price if it suits them, and not always without an eye to political expediency.
They take five years to pay us, and owe us nothing in the meantime.
If it were voluntary, we could call it a gift, but we would have no receipt for the income tax inspector.
We could not describe the Canadian people as being penniless and dependent upon charity.
We can only plead guilty to being a minority group.
These planners of our agricultural destiny like it very much, and now they want our oats and barley.
As they want complementary legislation from the prairie provinces, we should be able to block that, though there are powerful forces at work, whose aim it is to make the state all powerful, and reduce the status of the individual in like proportion.
I hope that you will continue to work toward the goal of getting back, not only our agricultural freedom, but the freedom of everyone who is yet a victim of government controls.
Yours truly,
R. H. Stevens, President, Farmers Protective Association.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: But it was your private enterprise that forced them to do that.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows very well what a failure the controller of feed has been. It he does not know that, I shall have to teach him. It is a thing that I know but which he does not seem to know. If there is anything that I know and he does not know, I shall take advantage of the opportunity to teach him a lesson.
Mr. Douglas is so anxious, as the socialist premier of Saskatchewan, to have this measure enacted to put oats and barley under the control of the wheat board that he is ready to send a representative to Ottawa. He communicated twice; I do not remember whether it was by letter or telegram, but that is of no consequence.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Carrier pigeon.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: He telegraphed or wrote twice to the minister telling him that he was ready to send one of his legal advisers by air to discuss the matter with the government at Ottawa and tell them what they would have to do with regard to oats and barley. This is planned economy. They start with oats and barley and will continue with rye and flaxseed; and then there will be no end. Why not do it as Stalin does right away? I have said many a time that socialism is the forerunner of communism.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: No, Liberalism is.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Surely.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
This is heresy. May I say to the hon. gentleman that, when he says that, he does not know what he is talking about. But now that they have a planned economy, they want to subject all the farmers of Canada to the rule of socialism, the rule of the C.C.F. I remember the time when Mr. Woodsworth and Miss Macphail suggested that the farmers should work eight hours a day. They did not go on with that for very

long. I remember the kind of agrarian reform they were preaching, and it was pure socialism. It meant the dispossession of the farmers who owned the lands in order to put them under a scheme that was quite similar to the one which has now been enforced in Russia. Then they changed and made great compromises with the farmers.
We are now discussing this grain business. I get into the closed reserve of the socialists of the west to tell them that they are wrong when they say they speak on behalf of the majority of the farmers of Canada, both from the west and from the east, when they try to impose socialist legislation on the government. I still hope that the minister will leave feed grain aside when he deals with the wheat business. One of my hon. friends the other day said to me, "You find prices high. You want controls on grain." I never wanted controls on grain. We cannot control the price of grain or the price of any other commodity by putting on an embargo when we need that commodity in this country, or by lifting that embargo when prices are too low. I do not object to the farmers selling their wheat at a reasonable price. I have said that before and I repeat it now. But when the coarse grain is harvested in a much smaller quantity than is normal, the department should see to it that the farmers of the east have an opportunity to buy that grain from the producers of the west. Otherwise what I shall do will be to tell the farmers of the east to become independent of the farmers of the west; not to buy their grain from them, but to harvest enough grain to be independent. We are ready to make concessions.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Do you think they can become independent?

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Surely they can do it. They can do it with regard to oats and barley. My hon. friend knows that very well. We can be independent of the farmers of the west. I do not know how long I shall have the pleasure of seeing the good-looking faces of my hon. friends in front of me in the house, but I will tell them that the farmers of the east are sick of that propaganda. They have had enough of it. The farmers of the east are ready to make concessions. They are ready to pay a fair price, provided that the goods are delivered to them, but they do not want to be the slaves of C.C.F. policy any more than do the farmers of the west.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Is the hon. member in favour of the eastern farmers receiving freight-free feed coming into the east, with the freight paid from the lakehead? Is the hon. member in favour of having freight paid on feed from the lakehead to the east for the eastern farmers?

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: It sounds good, does it not?

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: I have no objection to reasonable assistance. But if that subsidy is enforced, and the government is willing to pay that subsidy, then we want to have the goods in the east, and we want to have a different situation from the one we had last fall when all the farmers were complaining that they could not get delivery of the grain.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: It was your private enterprise that stopped delivery.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
It was not private enterprise. It was when we had a feed controller who is still there writing his memoirs. My hon. friends are so doctrinaire that they will not agree with me that it is a waste of money to keep that man in his job, especially after the situation for which he was responsible last fall.
I do not consider it a pleasure to rise tonight and to have to argue with hon. members from another province about this matter, which is a vital issue for us at the present time, but which may not be any longer a vital issue for us in the near future, when the farmers of the east are told of the difficulties that we have precisely on account of those controls.
Advice from a friend is much better than a suggestion from a foe. The wounds of those who love are better than the kisses of those who hate. This I dedicate to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe). And I will ask them both, after the performance that took place tonight, is it possible to say for one moment that the suggested policy of the government has been imposed upon them by the C.C.F. socialist group of Saskatchewan? There is no reply to that.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Your colleague from Ros-thern would be interested to hear that.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps he was too mild with his opponents.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Too frightened of them.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: He is too much of a good-natured fellow. That is why he has been lenient with these policies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will say who caused the Liberal government of 1922 to pass the wheat board legislation. The C.C.F. did not exist then.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, the C.C.F. did not exist; but Mr. Woodsworth was a member of the House of Commons at that time. My hon. friend will recall that Mr. Woodsworth was elected in 1921, and he was very powerful in connection with this matter, as well as many others whom I shall not now take time to enumerate.
What I want is a Liberal policy of free enterprise.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: This is a Liberal bill.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
It is a government bill. But I do not say it is a Liberal policy. I am not deceived by false labels, and this is why: knowing the sincerity of both the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, I urge upon them the necessity to stop the gap of socialism in this measure. We should do that for the good of the farmers of this country, and even for th$ good of the members from the west who are farmers themselves. They have been led to believe that socialist policies are opportune, that they are timely and that the government should make them their own. There is the correspondence which my hon. friend read the other day. There are all the speeches which have been made.
Tonight I listened with great interest to the excellent speech of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) who, although he is a lawyer, knows more about farming the west than does any member of the C.C.F. group. He has lived with the farmers and has listened to them.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: Whom do you think we live with? We are farmers.

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I was going to tell my hon. friend that if I were one of her constituents I would say many things to her, with the exception of talking about wheat. I would tell her that she is gifted and that she is doing well as a member of parliament. The only thing I regret in her is her obstinacy at times to admit that she may be wrong. I should like to be a poet to write a few rhymes for the hon. member. However, since I am not so well gifted I must say what I have to say in my poor language. But I mean well. And I hope that before long she will understand that my appeal to her reason has not been made in vain, and that perhaps she will be one who will canvass other members of the C.C.F. groups to drop their insistence upon passing this kind of legislation.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: I think the hon. member means that this goes against the grain. Does the hon. member recall what happened on August 29, 1946, as it is reported in Hansard at page 5598, when he read to the house his telegram to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) of August 28, 1939, and the Prime Minister's reply, and boasted that he was "responsible to a certain extent for the creation of the wartime prices and trade board"?

maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, since the hon. member speaks to me that way, I will tell him what happened. I was not going to say that, because he would think I was boasting. I will tell him that after that answer was sent to me by the Prime Minister I was called with the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to the office of the late Hon. Norman Rogers to form a committee of internal security to decide with him about food and commodity prices. There was
no question about wartime prices board here. Is that enough for the hon. member? I would not have said this, if my hon. friend had not given a false interpretation. Besides that, we were each offered $6,000 a year outside our indemnities. And I can tell the hon. member much more than that. I never have been for the wartime prices board, and it was only indirectly that I was responsible for its establishment some time afterwards.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
That was not the interpretation the hon. member gave when he read the telegram on August 29, 1946.
